Mr. ST. LAURENT: I take it, then, I have the unanimous consent of the house to have both resolutions considered at the same time, so that they both may be dealt with in the same remarks.
Although these trade agreements are negotiated and signed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I understand that it has been the practice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to move in the house the resolutions for approval of such agreements. In 1942 the Prime Minister explained that that practice had been adopted because the formalities for ratification and notification to the other contracting parties were handled through the Department of External Affairs.
These agreements are of the nature of agreements affording most favoured nation treatment between the countries which enter into them. They are similar to other trade agreements of which there have been several in recent years; as a matter of fact there were seven from 1937 to 1942. In 1937 there was a similar agreement between Canada and Uruguay, which was approved at the session of 1937. In 1938 two were approved, one with Guatemala and the other with Haiti. In 1940 the house gave approval to a similar agreement between Canada and the Dominican republic, and in 1942 the house approved of three similar agreements entered into between Canada and Chile, Canada and Brazil, and Canada and Argentina.
The two agreements now before the house are one more indication of the growing spirit of cordiality between Canada and the Latin republics. They will serve to strengthen the bonds of friendship which unite Canada and the two countries, and to facilitate further and to develop the commercial relations already existing, on a mutually profitable basis. Both trade agreements provide in general for most favoured nation treatment, and are similar to the trade agreements with the other Latin American nations. The trade agreement with Mexico was signed on February 8, at Mexico City and came into provisional effect on the same day. The trade agreement with Colombia was signed at Bogota on February 20 and will come into effect thirty days after the exchange
Trade Agreements

of ratifications. Both agreements are to remain in force for a period of two years, and to continue thereafter subject to termination on six months' notice. The trade agreement with Mexico provides for the exchange of most favoured nation treatment between the two countries in matters concerning duties and subsidiary charges, as -well as in respect of rules and formalities connected with importation and of laws and regulations affecting the taxation, sale, distribution or use of imported goods. This means in a general way that the products of each country, on importation into the other, will not be subject to customs duties or other charges greater than those applicable to similar imports from a third country. Similarly any reductions which either Canada or Mexico may grant in future to a third country will automatically be extended to the other. Thus imports into Canada from Mexico will in future, instead of being subject to the general tariff as heretofore, be . accorded the intermediate tariff, and any lower rates than the intermediate tariff granted by Canada to other foreign countries, with the exception of course of the imperial preferences. There is a special reservation in both treaties providing that arrangements between Canada and other dominions or colonies subject to the British crown are not affected. The tariff treatment now granted by Canada to other British countries is expressly excluded from the operation of the agreement.
No immediate reduction in customs duties is made by Mexico for goods of Canadian origin, as it has been Mexican policy not to limit the application of conventional duties to countries with which she has trade agreements. In other words, Mexico has a single column of duties applicable equally to imports from all countries, and any tariff reductions she has made in favour of a particular country, as for example those contained in the Mexico-United States trade agreement concluded- in 1942, already in practice have been extended to Canada.
An important provision of the agreement is that quantitative restrictions which may be imposed upon imports into either country from the other are subject to consultation. The agreement provides also that if either country sets up government agencies with exclusive privileges for exportation or importation of goods, such agencies will be influenced solely by consideration of price, quality, transportation and terms of purchase or sale which would ordinarily be taken into account by a private commercial enterprise.

Subject to certain specified exceptions, the new agreement provides that imports into either country from the other will be exempt from all internal taxes, fees, or charges other or higher than those payable on articles of national origin within the taxing country or of any other foreign origin. That is, there is to be no tax discrimination in this country on goods imported from Mexico, and vice versa. This provision will result in a reduction in the Mexican registration fees established by the Mexican department of health. Hitherto the fee for registration of packaged food products and beverages has been 50 pesos per product, and for pharmaceutical specialties and toilet preparations, 200 pesos per product, when imported from any country except the United States. That special charge is eliminated by virtue of this most favoured nation agreement. The fee for goods of both these categories of Mexican domestic origin or when imported from the United States is 20 pesos per product, and will now be the same for like products imported into Mexico from Canada. Under the new agreement, Canadian goods of these classes will also be entitled to the lower fee when submitted for registration in Mexico.
The trade agreement also provides that each country will grant the other an opportunity for consultation if either adopts any measure which is considered by the government of the other country as tending to nullify or impair any of the objects of the agreement. The operation of customs regulations, control of foreign exchange, quantitative restrictions and their administration, the observance of customs formalities and the application of sanitary laws and regulations all come within the scope of this provision of the agreement. If a satisfactory adjustment is not arrived at after consultation, the agreement may be terminated in whole or in part upon giving thirty days' notice.
The trade agreement, which is the first ever concluded between Canada and Mexico, came into force provisionally on February 8, the date of its signature. The provisional application may be terminated on three months' notice by either party. Thirty days after exchange of the instruments of ratification at Ottawa the trade agreement is to go into force definitely for two years. Its duration is automatically continued thereafter for one year periods, subject to termination on six months' notice by either party to the agreement.
It may perhaps be of some interest to hon. members to have an indication of the volume of trade between Canada and Mexico in recent years. For instance, in 1940 Canadian exports to Mexico amounted to $4,328,406 and our imports were only $733,797.

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. St. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the constitution of the world health organization signed at New York on July 22, 1946, and that -this house do approve the same.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen
would no doubt wish to have a few words, which will not be new to them but which will summarize the steps which led up to the formation of this world health organization.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONSTITUTION SIGNED AT NEW YORK, JULY 22, 1946.
speechtext:
Would it be possible to have a copy of the document?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The constitution was published as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings of July 24.
The steps leading up to the signature of the constitution of the world health organization in New York on July 22 were initiated, at the united nations conference at San Francisco when the word "health" was inserted in the charter upon the proposal of the delegation from Brazil. Following this action the states represented on the appropriate committee unanimously approved the following declara-

tion of Brazil and China, on the calling of an international conference for the purpose of establishing an international health organization.
The resolution thus unanimously approved was in the following terms:
The. delegations of Brazil and China recommend that a general conference be convened within the next few months for the purpose of establishing an international health organization.
They intend to consult further with the representatives of other delegations with a view to the early convening of such a general conference to which each of the governments here represented will be invited to send representatives.
They recommend that in the preparation of a plan for the international health organization full consideration be given to the relationship of such an organization, and methods of associating it with -other institutions, national as well as international, which already exist or which may hereafter be established in the field of health.
They recommend that the proposed international health organization be brought into relationship with the economic and social council.
Although the governments of Brazil and China followed up the declaration by suggesting that a conference be held before the end of 1945, the resolution relating to this proposal was not adopted by the economic and social council until February 15, 1946. In accordance with the terms of paragraph 3 of this resolution, the economic and social council established the technical preparatory committee and directed that it should meet in Paris not later than March 15, 1946, to prepare a draft annotated agenda and proposals for the consideration of the conference to be held not later than June 20, 1946.
At this point it might be useful to note what the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) said at the economic and social council of June 29, 1946. These were the words he used:
In the establishment of the economic and social council, in the setting up of its commissions, in the negotiation of relationships with the special purpose, agencies established by intergovernmental agreement, we are opening up a new chapter in the long struggle of mankind to master his environment, to the end that the material and economic resources of the world are used for the enrichment and not the destruction of humanity. Our task is not an easy one. We shall have to overcome not only the internal forces in various countries which resist change, but also the skepticism that we shall encounter in many parts of the world regarding the possibility of sucess in a cooperative effort of this sort.
I may say that these views, expressed thus by our Secretary of State at the international meeting, ap'peared to meet wit-h the unanimous approval of those to whom they were addressed.

World Health Organization
At the international health conference which met at the Henry Hudson hotel in New York city on June 19, 1946, the rapporteur of the technical preparatory committee, Major General G. B. Chisholm, presented a report which included proposals for the constitution of the world health organization. These proposals had been carefully worked out in Paris by this technical preparatory committee of experts, and they proved to be most useful documents.
The constitution of the world health organization will be found on page 9 of the addendum to the Votes and Proceedings of July 24.
Hon. .members will note in chapter 3 of the constitution that membership in the organization is open to all states. Conditions of admission, however, are governed by articles 4, 5 and 6 of the constitution. Fifty-one united nations attended the conference, and in addition the governments of Albania, Austria, Bulgaria, Eire, Finland, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Portugal, Siam, Sweden, Switzerland and Transjordan were represented by observers. The governments of the following states had also been invited to send observers but were not represented. Afghanistan, Roumania, Yeman. The Allied control authorities in Germany, Japan and Korea were represented by observers but without the right to vote. So were ten other international organizations.
Hon. members will note that article 19 deals with the powers of the health assembly to adopt conventions or agreements with respect to any matter within the competence of the organization, and article 20 imposes the obligation upon member states to take action relative to the acceptance or rejection of conventions or agreements proposed by the health assembly within eighteen months after the adoption of a convention or agreement.
A member is not bound to acquiesce in the convention or agreement, but if he does not accept the convention within the time limit he is required to furnish a statement of his reasons for non-acceptance to the director-general.
Article 21 gives the health assembly the authority to adopt regulations concerning five matters. It is stipulated in article 22 that such regulations shall come into force for all members after due notice has been given of their adoption by the health assembly, except for such members as may notify the director-general of ratification or reservation within the period stated in the notice.
With respect to article 21, A, B, D, and E, these refer to matters which were dealt with before by international agreement and sanitary conventions and by national legislation 63260-274
such as our food and drugs act. "A" refers to sanitary and quarantine requirements and other provisions designed to prevent the international spread of disease. "B" contains the nomenclatures with respect to diseases, causes of death and public health practices so that statistics supplied by the nations, members of the organization, may be comparable. "C" relates to standards with respect to diagnostic procedures for international use, and is perhaps more of professional and scientific than of general interest. "D" relates to standards with respect to the safety, purity and potency of biological, pharmaceutical and similar products moving in international commerce, and of course it is very important for the health of the world that such biological and pharmaceutical products which are distributed internationally be of standard quality and purity. "E" deals with advertising and labelling of biological, pharmaceutical and similar products moving in international commerce.
With respect to article 21C, that is to say, standards for diagnostic procedures for international use, this is a new departure, but it is felt that it can be beneficial to world understanding. From the Canadian viewpoint we have high standards of requirements for the safety and potency of pharmaceutical and biological products. The adoption of standards of requirements concerning them will not adversely affect us. If in the future some regulation should prove unacceptable to the government of Canada, the government can at any time contract out by giving notice, within eighteen months, of its desire to do so and of its reasons for so doing. It is felt that this will be one of the useful agencies of the international organization, and it is in line with the general purposes and aims of us all to strive for peace among men by making men realize what help they can receive from each other and to what extent it is beneficial to them all to be dependent upon one another.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONSTITUTION SIGNED AT NEW YORK, JULY 22, 1946.
speechtext:
The constitution of the international health conference, which has been placed before the house by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), is one of the most important documents that have ever been considered by the Canadian Parliament. If the nations of the world agree to establish a world health organization, then there is every hope for agreement in other matters.
The constitution, objective and functions as described in chapter I comprise a momentous decision on the part of the nations of the world. Never before in the history of the world have all the nations mutually agreed on a common plan for the betterment of the
World Health Organization

health conditions of humanity. It is only by united effort that the world may be cleansed and healed of the scourge of disease so prevalent in its past history, causing untold agonies and distress which to a great degree could have been avoided if such understanding among the nations of the world had been in effect decades ago.
The world is suffering from a malignant disease which causes loss of economic, social and spiritual values. We can effect a cure only by cultivating a spirit of cooperation among all peoples. This can best be done by banishing preventable disease, poverty, cold and hunger. We believe that in civilized society no man should be allowed to suffer or die from such causes, but it will be necessary to build a new world on the ruins of the old. Human rights must be restored and new confidence and tolerance must be established. The preservation of health must be international in scope, and science will aid in the upbuilding of the new world. More than ever before we must prevent and control disease and concern ourselves with the care of the handicapped and crippled, maternal and child care, the construction of hospitals, maintenance of health centres, the removal of the causes which predispose such large numbers of cases of mental illness, medical service to the poor, and other aspects of social security.
To provide health services for the people a government should give financial support, leadership and direction. In order to safeguard the state, its people must be as physically and mentally fit as it is possible to make them. There should be no economic or geographic boundaries in equality of opportunity for medical care. The aims of the science of healing should be international and the same over all the world. Canada must take her place along with similar organizations in other nations in preventing wars and giving adequate health services to all people. The present is an opportune time to form an intenational organization whose first Object is to give better health and medical services to all people. Millions of the people of the world are suffering physically and mentally as a result of the war. A united nations health organization would provide much toward the welfare and future happiness of mankind. Now that military victory in Europe has been achieved, peace will bring many difficult problems for solution. We can best solve these problems and reach a better understanding by the relief of suffering.
The pages of the history of our own country, when studied from the aspect of health, show many occasions on which disease itself con-

trolled the destiny of a young and growing nation. Few are aware that it played a major role in the mastery of the North American continent, in the wars between France and England.. Repeatedly it decimated the population and seriously retarded the development of the country. A person who has not taken full account of the diseases which afflicted this country and of the efforts to stay their ravages does not know the full history of Canada. Had it not been for disease that plagued the French settlers from the time of their arrival in the country, it is doubtful whether Canada would have become a British possession. Contagious diseases were rapidly introduced by shipping from the earliest days and recurred in epidemic form at frequent intervals. We look upon influenza as a disease of modern civilization, yet there were many outbreaks in Canada in- the early days. It appeared at regular interval® and there are many records of it. In 1918 it eclipsed all previous records, causing 30.000 deaths in Canada, Like many other diseases it was introduced by shipping and spread throughout the whole country, at least- one-sixth of the population being affected. If disease can control the destiny of Canada, it may well control the world.
We in- Canada have failed to learn our lesson from the past. In the examination of recruits for the war just ended thirty-five to forty per cent of our young men were found unfit for service. A high percentage of these defects for which they were rejected could have been eliminated by early and proper treatment. The infant mortality in our own country is fifty-four per thousand live births. In this regard I give the following statistics of infant mortality in other countries, all of which have a lower rate than we have in Canada:

There were 798 maternal deaths in Canada in 1943. I call attention to the large number of deaths from tuberculosis and cancer within

World Health Organization
our dominion. The elimination of venereal disease stands as a challenge to all Canadians working in the field of public health. The high death rate from cancer should call for all means to be used in research for cure. Death and disease do not wait for a gradual extension of science. Death and suffering of the people, while life is within reach, is a human cruelty and an affront to mankind's conscience. The fights against maternal mortality, against the maiming and death caused by infantile paralysis, against tuberculosis and venereal disease, are fights for the whole Canadian nation. Science is a factor in the battle against maternal mortality and in the prevention of infantile paralysis with its terrible crippling effects. Modern research has made, and is now making, tremendous progress in every major disease, but these methods are not being used in the cure of disease for all of the population. If . money can be obtained to wipe out such disease which it costs us millions to maintain, then within a generation there will no longer be this drain upon the wealth of our nation. This is one way to ease our tax burden. The insulin research of Banting and the workers associated with him cost less than $10,000. The Rockefeller Foundation gave Howard Florry $1,280 for apparatus which helped solve problems in the production of penicillin. If one per cent of the annual cost of disease were given to trained researchers, much could be done to improve health in this country and save the colossal sums spent annually on disease.
The cost of prevention of disease, now possible, thanks to modern medicine, is nothing compared to the terrific present cost of supporting people through long years of unproductive sickness. It costs more to let them be disabled than it would cost to keep them in good health and let them earn their own living.
Of the twenty-two clauses of functions in the draft of the united nations health organization, there is not one open to debate or criticism. It would be impossible to discuss all of them in the time allotted. I shall refer to one or two items:
Clause A states:
The health assembly shall have authority to adopt regulations concerning sanitary and quarantine requirements and other procedures designed to prevent the international spread of disease.
This is most important to the protection of our own country. Owing to modern methods of travel and the shortness of time required to make a journey, persons suffering from contagious disease might land in this country during the incubation stage before the disease was apparent.
The promotion of research and interchange of scientific data will lead to important discoveries being made by the scientists of the world. It may well be that a bacteriologist in far off Australia may discover a cure or treatment for infantile paralysis, and that as a result of his efforts little children in Canada will not be crippled.
A scientist in his laboratory in Europe may discover a treatment for cancer and thus save suffering and death from a disease which kills one person in eight of the population of Canada.
The extent of cooperation outlined in the resolution is of such magnitude that it is difficult to believe. But one fact is outstanding, that in the present troubled state of the peoples of the world more will be accomplished by the world health organization to promote peace and good will than by any other agency in the power of the nations. Ignorance and prejudices will be broken down by healing the sufferings of humanity. During the war we glibly talked of the new world to be built after victory. Let us build that new world by a combined effort to eliminate disease and misery. I appeal to the members of the Canadian parliament to support this resolution unanimously.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that, all hon. members will be glad to support this motion and that we are all agreed on the objective as set out in article 1:
The objective of the world health organization shall be the attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health.
I think the definitions are very well set out, too, under the constitution. I particularly like the second paragraph, which says:
The enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition.
Much careful thought has gone into the drawing up of this very fine constitution, and I only hope that we shall live up to the expectations of those who drafted it. I am reminded of the tragedy of the labour convention at Geneva where twenty-six years ago Canada endorsed the eight-hour day, and in Canada we are still striking to attain it. I hope we do not do that with our health commitments; otherwise a lot of people are going to die in the meantime.
As I see it, Canada has two sets of responsibilities: first, to support this organization and take full part in it, to see that we have full representation and that we share the financial obligation, and to ensure that nothing is left
World Health Organization

undone in the sharing of research, and second, to clean up Canada. Canada has made some splendid contributions to the attack on disease. When we think of Sir Frederick Banting and his gift of insulin; when we think of the record we have set in the matter of the onslaught on tuberculosis, which a few years ago was one of the great scourges from which mankind suffered, I believe it will be agreed that we too have helped to write medical history. I am reminded of the history of our attack on tuberculosis, and in the province from which I come we have established, I believe, a world record. We found there that there were social factors which made it possible to do this, and the most important of all was the controlled environment of the patient. When we began to treat tuberculosis we did not only look after the medical end of it; we looked after housing and nutrition. The patient in a tuberculosis sanatorium gets the very finest of food-unlimited quantities of fruit and meat and milk, the best of housing, of heating, of sanitation and everything else that contributes to healthful surroundings. There, I think, we have one of the keys of the attack on disease-the controlled environment of the individual. But so long as we in Canada have slums, overcrowding, obsolete and unsanitary buildings, ignorance and poverty, we shall sustain these losses from disease, preventable losses which we can avoid by attacking the living conditions of our people. So I hope not only that we shall sign this covenant and pledge ourselves to international health, but that we shall not rest until every Canadian family has healthful, sanitary home surroundings.
I see here that we have had seven different conventions on sanitation. I wish I had the figures to show how many families in this country still do not have sanitary conveniences. There is a great field of activity open to us, if we are interested in sanitation, in seeing to it that every family has plumbing and running water, a clean water supply, sufficient space, good beds, good clothing, and laundry facilities. These are the very essence of cleanliness and health, and in this direction we can make a really worth while contribution.
I believe we are very fortunate in our minister of health and that he is doing excellent work. However, this parliament should extend to the provinces grants under the provisions which were suggested in the original proposals, to allow the provinces through their departments of health to make an attack on the various aspects of public health-the mental diseases, the venereal diseases, tuberculosis-and to establish a special division of child and maternal welfare. I hope
(Mrs. Strum.]
that very soon the Minister of Finance will see fit to extend to the provinces that are going to sign these agreements individually the same assistance which the original proposals contain, because we all know that health is a provincial matter, that it must be paid for in cold dollars and cents, and that it is for sale; that there are millions of people to-day suffering from disease, and thousands in this country doomed to die because they have not the price of medical attention. For them health is unavailable, and until we make health services free, thousands of people are doomed to die of cancer, for instance, because they cannot afford expensive surgery. Only one province that I know of has completely eliminated personal cost from the treatment of cancer. When we have made it possible for the provinces to carry out their programmes of health we can begin to feel that we in Canada have done our part towards realization of the dream of the great men who drew up this charter.

Mr. Speaker, the motion of the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) is a most laudable one, but I say to him that this interim agreement, followed by a constitution of a world health organization establishing certain definite principles, should not be treated as Canada dealt with the public health convention of 1927, the international sanitary convention which is referred to in this schedule and was concluded on June 21, 1926. I remember being in the house at that time, and I was of opinion that Canada should take an active part regarding the health of the world, and for the reasons expressed in this constitution:
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
The enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition.
The health of all peoples is fundamental to the attainment of peace and security and is dependent upon the fullest cooperation of individuals and states.
The achievement of any state in the promotion and protection of health is of value to all.
Unequal development in different countries in the promotion of health and control of disease, especially communicable disease, is a common danger.
The convention goes on to describe many branches of public health. But what has Canada since 1926? As a nation we have merely given lip service to these ideals. We spent only half a million dollars, and the promotion of public health in Canada has

World Health Organization
been left largely to hospitals, public and private, to the universities and the municipalities. Since 1926 in some municipalities we have had to mark up from $1 to $2.50 a day for per diem patients. It was about the time of the 1926 convention that Doctor Banting wanted to go to the United States to practice -he had started practice in London-and to carry on the researches which led to his great discovery of the treatment of diabetes. The night before last I was looking at his grave in Mount Pleasant cemetery, marked only by a small tombstone. When one thinks of what this one invention and discovery in medicine and science did for the soldiers of the war from which we have just emerged, it is a revelation and a promise of what scientific research can do.
There have been many long discussions on the minister's health estimates in this house concerning public health. Long ago I urged here a forward national health policy. One of the mistakes made at confederation was the failure to foresee the need for a national health policy along the lines set out, first in the convention of 1926, and now in the interim convention which was only adopted on July 22 of this year. It is to be hoped that we shall now go into the matter in a practical way; in 1926 we only paid lip service to it. Let us do something practical now with the $14,000,000 voted here for public health. As I said in the debate on the estimates, the first duty of the government is to look after the health, peace, happiness and prosperity of its people. When I go around the country and see some of the conditions and the lack of aid to health departments I am surprised. When the municipal people ask for something, nothing is given.
National public health is looked after only by the municipalities, and the municipalities have to establish at great cost their own health departments without federal aid. It is the most important national work we have. If we are to join all these world organizations we shall be roaming all over America. We are on the seven seas in the first two resolutions. If this resolution carries we are bound by everything in it and the new constitution and all that happens in this world society, so the estimates on public health may run into millions of dollars. It is all done by resolution. I contend that that is not right. I often look up the rules of the house. The two motions we have passed dealt with pan-American matters of trade, and they will interfere with British preferences.
There is to be a convention meeting next year on world trade. I ask lion, members to be very careful before they go into these
things. More estimates and votes will be needed in the countries which made this agreement on July 22. Hon. members will well remember a picture contained in the Ottawa Journal which I held up in the house one night, showing the delegates to the New York health meeting. We had about fifteen or twenty people from Canada at this health convention, but there was nobody representing the provinces. The minister was accompanied by what I describe as a small choir, but the health officers of the provinces were not there. They should have been there because they will have to carry out the terms of the text of the interim constitution. The great universities of the country which have made such rapid strides, in peace and war alike, in medicine, science, physics and chemistry and everything else, should have been consulted. I read a copy of the proceedings of this New York meeting which appeared in the New York Times and I find no reference to the universities or to provincial health officers.
While I support the principle of the policy I believe that Canada should stop giving lip loyalty to all these things which will necessitate our voting large sums of money to be used by these bodies. When I first came to the house the problem with regard to agriculture was, where shall the hired man wash his feet. I have never known a minister of agriculture to solve that problem. Now we are going into the tremendous field of international health and medicine and all these things covered by communicable diseases and the other matters set out in. the interim constitution. All this is being done in Canada at a time when not one cent is given to the support of hospitals or to the universities as scholarships so that men of science such as we have in the universities of Toronto, McGill, Queen's, Western and the great university in British Columbia, the great university down by the sea and the other universities of the country, could continue their studies. There is where the mistake was made at confederation. The British North America Act should have made health and education concurrent jurisdiction. We are giving only lip loyalty to these health matters federally. The department is only a skeleton department. If we are to go into this matter let us adopt some new national policy. When we pass this resolution we shall not know what it is going to cost. We had a similar resolution before us in 1926, and we do not know what Canada has done because she left national public health to the hospitals, the universities, municipalities, the medical profes-
World Health Organization

sion, the dental profession and all these other bodies without a vote or any help from the department here.
As I say for several weeks we were represented at this New York convention by the minister, and he had fourteen or fifteen with him, a regular choir. Their task was to represent the department. I do hope that we shall have something practical, done for the health of the country by the provision of more hospitals, nurses and doctors. Two floors have been closed in the Toronto general hospital because of the lack of nurses. All this is going on, but Canada does nothing. Let us improve national health in this country. I am not opposed to the resolution; I supported, it in 1926. The principles of federal aid which guided Doctor Hastings, Toronto's great health officer, are the principles which I express now. He was a leader and a pioneer on health matters at these international conventions which met in the states, after the last war and all over the world.
The British medical association, the body which did more than any other agency for science along the terms of this new constitution, and the various medical associations of the dominions and of the United States, have done great work along these lines. I hope that the time has come-it has to come next year according to the terms of this constitution-for us to be up and doing. It will cost S5 million a year. I ask hon. members to be careful of how they tie us up because the money must be voted by the committee of supply if we adopt the constitution. The money could, be far better spent in Canada where it is badly needed in many ways.
They talk in this agreement about a pure water supply, and all that kind of thing. Impure water is the basis of typhoid, diphtheria, and many other communicable diseases. I remember that Vancouver had a little trouble about sanitation and1 filtration. We have had in our city a pure water supply for twenty-five years. We set it up by 'building a large water filtration system, and since then there have been practically no cases of typhoid and only five or six of diphtheria. At onetime in Toronto, owing .to the collapse of an intake, they were drinking water from the bay.
One of the most important clauses in the constitution will run into hundreds of millions of dollars because it deals with communicable diseases and many new diseases, and new drugs, the use of which is killing some people. We shall have to -be careful about the constitution. Where are the provinces in this convention?^ I think it is important to see that the provinces are consulted and also the larger
[Mr. Church.!
municipalities. Toronto city spends five or six times more than this department of health. The federal department here went from $200,000 to $500,000 before the war, and in the estimates we passed, the other day the amount was $14,000,000.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance said that we want all these things, but let us remember that they cost money. Let us go into it with our eyes open. We are simply giving lip service by passing all these resolutions in one morning without knowing how they interfere with the plans of the provinces and the municipalities. Every one of the diseases mentioned in the meeting in New York dealt with by the universities and the health officers of Canada many years ago. They were pioneers in this work. Canada was a pioneer, following the principles of the mother country, the United States and the dominions.
This particular agreement was lying on the desk of the Minister of National Health and Welfare on his estimates the night he left. I took part in the debate myself, along with many other hon. members. This agreement should have been considered at that time and all the details given.

Before the resolution carries I wish to point out what I believe to be the justifiable and commendable trend in national and international affairs exhibited in the adoption by this nation and several others of the constitution of the health conference. This trend, now becoming accelerated, portends the making of a better world for which all of us have been striving during these years, and points to our giant objective. It is the placing of a broader emphasis and value upon human needs in. relation to material affairs. If ever there was a time when it was possible to see clearly the movement in world affairs I think it is to-day, when I believe we are finally coming to the point of relegating the strictly material things, such as property values, to a position of importance second to human rights, human values and humanity in general. I welcome a move of this kind as another step in the right direction; that is, to a more progressive position in our world relationships.
This is a great test of international cooperation. I had the privilege of listening to Senator Warren Austin, the new voice of the United States of America on the security council, before he took his place on that couiv cil, when he addressed the New York branch of the foreign policy association. Significantly enough, it was the anniversary of the signing of the San Francisco charter. I think per-

World Health Organization
haps one of the most vital and compelling things he said was that nations still have a long way to go to find a formula by which they can get along, but that health is one of the universal things which may well be used as a testing ground, something in which people of all nations have a common interest and a common objective. I find myself, and I am quite sure this house finds itself, largely in agreement with that point of view. Let us work on those things upon which the nations of the world can more readily agree. Let us work on those first, in a comprehensive way, in order to find, if possible, a formula for dealing with the more difficult problems that lie ahead. This is a testing ground, because health knows no boundaries, health knows no creed, health knows no nationality or limitation. It is a great human relationship which brings the world together from time to time.
It was my privilege to attend for a short period the world conference in New York which has been mentioned already in this debate, and to see arriving for those deliberations great and eminent surgeons and physicians from the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, from the United States of America, from the United Kingdom, from France and from the smaller nations of the world. There I saw a young plastic surgeon, twenty-five years of age, already with great experience; and to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) I would say she was one of the prominent lady surgeons and physicians who came from all over the world to play a prominent part at the conference. There we had a great pooling of brains in matters affecting surgery,, medicine and public health. To me it was a great and practical example of how the world may finally discover that much sought after formula for a means of living together as good neighbours the world over.
I believe this movement for a world health organization can be pretty well expressed in this sort of phraseology. Those of us who come from the rural parts of Canada realize that no matter how clean you keep your own farm, no matter what measures you take for weed prevention, that is not enough unless your neighbour keeps his farm clean as well. The world health organization represents an effort to see that the weeds all over the world, on our neighbour's land as well as our own, are cleaned up in the interests of all. Without putting it on the lower level of our own selfish interest, it is important that the disease-infested swamps of the world be drained and cleaned up, in our own interests
as well as the interests of those in whose lands the swamps are to be found. I know most of us are interested in the success of the united nations health organization, because success in an endeavour like this goes far in preparing the way for international cooperation on all fronts. Of course the united nations organization has given us cause for some disappointment as well as some optimism; but in the final analysis, like any other organization or any individual, the united nations organization and its various component parts must deliver the goods; and when they have delivered the goods they will have world support. That is why I think we are fortunate in Canada to be one of the first nations to nake a move to adopt a constitution such as fiiis. It is a forward step toward a better world, a better humanity. It lays greater emphasis upon the right things of life which in the end will be the deciding points as between peace or war, content or suffering, joy or sorrow in the days to come..

It has been interesting to listen to the debate thus far, Mr. Speaker. I have been impressed by the fact that most of those who have participated up to the present time have given reasons why we in Canada should pay much more attention to our health problems, but no reasons why we should join an international organization to accomplish that objective. Apart from such things as quarantine regulations, you might say, it is difficult to see how joining an international organization is going to help us solve the problems which are vital in dealing with our health situation. I greatly enjoyed the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), but in them there was hardly anything to indicate why we should join this international organization, or that to do so would necessarily advance our interests in respect to health. I hope after a while in the house and in the country we may begin to be a little more realistic than we have shown ourselves to be in the last year or so. There seems to be abroad in the land an idea that any problem under the sun can be solved if you can get it far enough away from yourself and into the hands of a big enough international organization. I am really a bit surprised that no one has suggested sending a delegation to Mars, one to Jupiter, one to the moon, and delegations to three or four other planets, to see if we cannot set up an interplanetary organization to solve the problems of the world. That would seem a logical proposal, and I am somewhat disappointed that it has not been brought forward up to the present time.
World Health Organization

This sort of thing simply tends to take our minds off the real difficulties that confront us. Problems' of health in a large measure have to do with the standard of living. Whether joining this international organization for health will enable us to improve our standard of living in Canada, no one has taken pains to explain. Yet it is obvious from what has been said by everyone who has participated in the debate that the real cause of most of our ill health is a poor standard of living in Canada. Will anyone who is so ardently enthusiastic about this organization explain to me how signing the agreement will help us to raise our standard of living in Canada? That is what I want to know.
As I have already pointed out to the house on one or two earlier occasions, in the year preceding June 2, 1941, in Canada 32-9 per cent of our wage earners received less than $450 a year. Until we can change that situation we are simply making ourselves ridiculous, when we spend our time signing international organization agreements to promote health. In that same year another 28-7 per cent of our wage earners were receiving between $450 and $949 a year. A large percentage of the people earning those incomes were heads of families.
I am informed the Toronto welfare council has recently told the people of Canada that for a family to live under conditions of standard health and decency it will require in the neighbourhood of $2,000 a year. What I fear is that hon. members are getting their minds off the essentials that are right nearby. It is a common failing among human beings everywhere, and among organizations of human beings, to dream about the big things to be done by and by, while they neglect the little things around their feet which they might do something about.
There is no doubt that Canada can give to every person in Canada enough of the world's goods to supply a reasonable standard of health and decency. Judging from our national income and the production of our nation there is no reason for our being unable to have a doctor come to visit -regularly; there is no reason why we should not have a dentist attending the children regularly; there is no reason why every 'Canadian citizen should not have all the food he needs, well-balanced and well-prepared. There is no reason why they should not have the clothing and shelter they need.
As I recall it, in his report of 1946 Mr. Graham Towers told us that in 1944 we in Canada produced 11-8 billion dollars worth of goods and services, and in 1945 we profVr. Blackmore.]
duced 11 -4 billion. This was at a time when we had 1,500,000 of our very best potential producers engaged in war. If we take that amount of goods and services and divide it among 12 million people we find that we get in the neighbourhood of $916 per man, woman and child in Canada. Will anyone tell me why we have such a low standard of living among our people? Will anyone tell me how in the world by joining any number of international organizations like this one we can overcome that difficulty? If he will, I shall be interested immediately.
I have no desire to delay the house in a discussion of this matter. But I do hope we shall not get our eye off the ball by chasing rainbows or soap bubbles. By way of diversion I -would draw the attention of hon. members for a moment to the dismal disappointment we have had as a result of joining the united nations organization. A year ago one might have thought that by doing so we would go right into the millennium. Anyone who said we should not join it was held out as a public enemy. Yet, what have we got out of it?
Let us be realistic. Let us face the facts as they are and see if we cannot get down to earth. Let us begin walking on terra firma- on the rocks, the dirt and the mud-so that we shall have a sense of reality in these matters.
The group with which I am associated has no particular objection to joining this international health organization. But we warn that the more of our national affairs we allow either directly or indirectly to be influenced by bodies of people outside our country, the more difficult our situation is going to become. What we must learn is to manage our own country, to run our own business, to clean our own back yard. As soon as we learn how to do that, there will be plenty of people looking over our boundaries to find out how we have done it, We shall not need to go hunting people to teach; they will find us, and come to learn.
I have gone through the agreement, so far as I have had time to do so in conjunction with the many burdens placed upon me-as they are, of course, upon all other hon. members. I do not see in this constitution anything indicating a dangerous amount of control over our national affairs which could be exercised directly or indirectly by the government of this organization. If I could see any evidence that such a possibility was implicit in the organization I would oppose it with all the power at my command, and would call on all hon members to do the same. As it is, I

United Nations-Education
think it amounts almost to another bubble, another rainbow to go chasing after, and by which to be deluded.
Our group will not oppose this resolution; we will allow it to slide through. But let me repeat that it i^ time we got down to earth and began to find out the real cause of the troubles from which we suffer. Let us find out why in a country like Canada, which has produced goods valued at 11-8 billions of dollars, 32-9 per cent of our wage earners receive less than S450 a year, thus making it utterly impossible for them, and for any of those connected with them, to have health. If I might bring in another illustration which comes to mind, I would mention that I am now engaged in the industrial relations committee. Why in the world is it that we in Canada are risking the whole economic welfare of the country by resisting the desire of a group of men to make SI,750 a year as a minimum?
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his remarks are not relevant to the motion before the house.

I have all the deference for you and your opinion, Mr. Speaker, but not a single word of what I have uttered could possibly be said to be irrelevant to the matter of health in this country. Nor can it be irrelevant to the health of the world-not one word. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is the position in which your ruling puts the whole situation in this country.
I refrain from saying any more.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONSTITUTION OF EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the constitution of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization signed at London, on November 16, 1945, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: I do not think I could say anything more effective in support of this motion than to put on Hansard the preamble to the constitution of the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization:
The governments of the states parties to this organization on behalf of their peoples declare:
That since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed; that ignorance of each other's way and lives has been a common cause, throughout the history of mankind, of that suspicion and mistrust between the peoples of the world through which their differences have all too often broken into war; that the great and
terrible war which has now ended was a war made possible by the denial of the democratic principles of the dignity, equality and mutual respect of men, and by the propagation, in their place, through ignorance and prejudice, of the doctrine of the inequality of men and races; that the wide diffusion of culture, and the education of humanity for justice and liberty and peace are indispensable to the dignity of man and constitute a sacred duty which all the nations must fulfil in a spirit of mutual assistance and concern; that a peace based exclusively upon the political and economic arrangements of governments would not be a peace which could secure the unanimous, lasting and sincere support of the peoples of the world, and that the peace must therefore be founded, if it is not to fail, upon the intellectual and moral solidarity of mankind.
For these reasons, the states parties to this constitution, believing in full and equal opportunities for education for all, in the unrestricted pursuit of objective truth, and in the free exchange of ideas and knowledge, are agreed and determined to develop and to increase the means of communication 'between their peoples and to employ these means for the purposes of mutual understanding and a truer and more perfect knowledge of each other's lives. In consequence whereof they do hereby create the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization for the purpose of advancing, through the educational, scientific and cultural relations of the peoples of the world, the objectives of international peace and of the common welfare of mankind for which the united nations organization was established and which its charter proclaims.
It is the organization having these aims, and set- up for that purpose that this resolution invites this house of parliament to approve and in which it authorizes participation.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONSTITUTION OF EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Before the minister resumes his seat may I ask a question?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	I shall have no
objection to answering any questions I can when I have concluded.
The constitution was drafted by representatives of forty-four states meeting at an educational and cultural conference in London in November, 1945. At this meeting Canada was represented by a delegation consisting of the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, Principal R. C. Wallace of Queen's university and Mr. Edmond Turcotte, then editor of the Montreal newspaper Le Canada. The delegation's advisers were drawn from the Department of External Affairs, the education branch of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and the National Research Council.
The London meeting was the culmination of years of study and. thought by various international bodies seeking to promote the international and moral solidarity of mankind, believing, in the words of the preamble to the constitution, that "since wars begin in the minds of men it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed."

United Nations-Education

After the last war the importance of intellectual cooperation was appreciated and resulted in the creation of the international institute of intellectual cooperation which, through the generosity of the French government, was given headquarters in Paris. The international bureau of education in Geneva, also established in this period, likewise reflected the recognition of the need for some international cooperation through education. More and more international societies of scholars, scientists and artists began to meet at regular intervals to profit by friendly exchanges of ideas, but the development of totalitarian philosophies certainly impeded the growth and much of what was hoped from that development.
The second world war intensified the feeling that international intellectual cooperation was essential, and as early as September, 1941, Viscount Cecil took the lead in forming the London international assembly. A year later the first conference was held of the allied ministers of education which began to plan for the educational and cultural reconstruction of occupied countries. As this conference studied the problems of educational reconstruction in the occupied countries, it realized that it was necessary to go even further in promoting international cooperation in educational and cultural matters. The same need was realized in the United States where an unofficial education assembly in 1943 drew up plans for an international organization for educational and cultural development. In 1944 the United States proposals were discussed at the conference of allied ministers of education and a draft constitution was produced.
The British government then agreed to invite the allied governments to a conference to discuss this constitution in November, 1945. At the San Francisco meeting general endorsement was given of the resolution presented by France on cultural cooperation, and in the charter of the united nations, article I, section 3, full endorsement was given to the principle of promoting international, cultural and educational cooperation.
The nations at San Francisco, under the charter, also pledged themselves to take joint and separate action for the achievement of this purpose. The approval of the constitution of UNESCO, drafted in London in the fall of 1945, has already been given by seventeen countries. These include the United States of America and the members of the British commonwealth of nations-with the exception so far of Canada-Brazil, China, Denmark, the Dominican republic, France, Iran, Mexico,

Norway, Saudi-Arabia, Syria and Turkey. It is fully expected that the required number of twenty nations will have ratified the constitution before the first formal meeting of UNESCO takes place in Paris in November of this year. In the interval, since the drafting of the constitution, plans for its organization have been developed under the auspices of the executive committee on which Canada has been represented, and by the preparatory commission.
A distinguished British scientist, Doctor Julian Huxley, has been appointed as secretary of UNESCO. The agreement defining the relations of UNESCO with the economic and social council of the united nations has been drawn up and will be considered at the meeting of the united nations in September of this year.
The organization has been given functions which I will not take time to read to the house, but which if I might have the consent of hon. members I would put on Hansard in order to give continuity to my remarks on this resolution.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONSTITUTION OF EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Agreed.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The following functions have been given to the organization:
(a)	to collaborate in the work of advancing the mutual knowledge and understanding of peoples, through all means of mass communication and to that end recommend such international agreements as may be necessary to promote the free flow of ideas by word and image;
(b)	to give fresh impulse to popular education and to the spread of culture; by collaboration with members, at their request, in the development of educational activities; by instituting collaboration among the nations to advance the ideal of equality of educational opportunity without regard to race, sex, or any distinctions, economic or social; by suggesting educational methods best suited to prepare the children of the world for responsibilities of freedom.
(c)	to maintain, increase and diffuse knowledge; by assuring the conservation and protection of the world's inheritance of books, works of art and monuments of [DOT] history and science, and recommending to the nations concerned the necessary international conventions; by encouraging cooperation among the nations in all branches of intellectual activity, including the international exchange of persons active in fields of education, science and culture and the exchange of publications, objects of artistic and scientific interest and other materials of information; by initiating methods of international cooperation calculated to give the people of all countries access to the printed and published materials produced by any of them.
In carrying out these functions, UNESCO, must not interfere within the domestic jurisdiction of its members.

United Nations-Education
These purposes are safeguarded by section 3 of article 1, which is in the following terms:
With a view to preserving the independence, integrity and fruitful diversity of the cultures and educational systems of the states members of this organization, the organization is prohibited from intervening in matters which are essentially within their domestic jurisdiction.
The organization includes a general conference, an executive board and a secretariat. The general conference consists of not more than five delegates from each member state and will meet annually to determine the policy of the organization. From the conference may come recommendations and international conventions for the consideration of the member states. Each member state is under obligation to submit such recommendations and conventions to its competent authorities within one year, but is under no obligation whatsoever to acquiesce if it does not think it is wise to do so. The executive board consists of eighteen members elected by the general conference for terms of three years. Members may serve not more than two consecutive terms. It is the duty of the executive board to carry out the programme laid down by the conference and, for this purpose, it is to meet at least twice a year. The elected members of the board are to be drawn from "persons competent in the arts, the humanities, the sciences, education and the diffusion of ideas, and qualified by their experience and capacity to fulfil the administrative and executive duties of the board." The election should also take into account the diversities of cultures and a balanced geographical distribution. The secretariat consists of a director general and such staff as may be required.
Each member state is required to make arrangements in accordance with its particular conditions for linking up principal bodies interested in educational, scientific and cultural matters with the work of the organization. It is suggested that this preferably be done by forming a national commission which would be broadly representative of the government and such bodies. The national commission or some such body is intended to act in an advisory capacity to the government and to delegations to the general conference. It is also intended to be a liaison between various educational and cultural organizations and the government.
Here in Canada we have not yet determined what form of action we will take to bring the bodies interested in educational, scientific and cultural advancement into relationship with this international organization.

In the United States before the adjournment of congress a bill was adopted and signed by the president providing for the setting up in the United States of a national commission comprising one hundred members. Of course we would not have in contemplation anything as elaborate as that, but because of the jurisdiction of the provinces in matters of education we wish to confer with them as well as with the private organizations that exist for the promotion of educational, scientific and cultural development. It is desired to have some Canadian body that will be widely representative of the Canadian public and that will be entirely divorced from any partisan political influence, to make this a matter in which all those in Canada interested in educational, scientific and cultural development will feel that they have a part.
The precise financial relationship between the budget of UNESCO and the budget of the united nations has yet to be defined. A supplementary agreement is to be negotiated for that purpose between the two organizations. The view of the Canadian government is that the united nations should exercise a general supervision over UNESCO budgetary arrangements. It is also its view that caution should be taken in outlining financial commitments until UNESCO has had some experience in securing the cooperation of existing international organizations and societies in the educational, scientific and cultural fields. UNESCO is authorized with the approval of the executive board to receive gifts, bequests and subventions directly from governments, public and private institutions, associations and private persons.
The economic and social council is the liaison agent for the united nations with UNESCO. As mentioned previously, a draft agreement outlining this relationship was signed on June 4, in New York, subject to the action of the united nations in September and to that of the general conference of UNESCO in November. UNESCO will also consult and cooperate with other international organizations which presumably might include the atomic energy commission, the security council, though this is less likely, and the international labour organization.
It is one of those organizations designed -to bring into, cooperative relations those who are interested all over the world in educational, scientific and cultural development and, like the world health organization. human values as more important than mere material things, will enable them to work together to bring about- that state of mind where there will be less inquiring "who is my neighbour?" and more of a recognition that all men are of all men each other's neighbours.

Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, in the terms of the present resolution this house is asked to approve the

constitution of the united: nations educational, scientific and cultural organization signed at London on November 16, 1945. I for one trust that the resolution will have the unanimous endorsement of the house.
May I first deal with the point which was raised by the last question. Actually in the paper to which the Minister of Justice and Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), has just referred, treaty series 1945, No. 18, there are three documents. The first is the final act of the conference which met at London in November last; the second is the constitution of the organization commonly called UNESCO, and the third is the instrument establishing the preparatory commission looking forward to launching the new organization and putting it in running order. All that the house is asked to approve, as I understand it, in this present resolution is the second of these documents, namely the constitution of the organization.
I should like to point out that forty-four nations participated in the conference at London. Russia, as has been mentioned, along with the two Soviet republics which are granted separate international representation-the Ukraine republic and the Byelo-Russian republic-were not represented. Of the forty-four nations which attended the conference, forty-three signed the final act. Only El Salvador refrained from signing the final act. As for the constitution of the organization, thirty-nine nations signed. Those which did not sign were: El Salvador, Australia, France, New Zealand and the. United States of America. As for the third document, the instrument establishing the preparatory commission, forty-one nations signed; the three abstainers were El Salvador, Australia and France. It is a matter of general regret that this conference was not attended by any representatives of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics or the two other Soviet republics to which I have referred, and that there has been no indication from the Soviet union of any intention as yet of participating in this UNESCO organization.
I think that at the outset we should see this organization in its true perspective. It is established, as has been indicated, as one of those specialized agencies which were contemplated when the economic and social council of the united nations organization was brought into being; and it is in measures such as this, the setting up of specialized agencies of this kind, with the aim of ensuring peace by eliminating the ultimate causes of war, that much of the hope of the world for the future lies.

United Nations-Education
It is to be seen that in the approach to this agenci*s of this kind, with the aim of ensuring that peace must be constructed on a broad basis, that there must be the broadest possible approach to the problem of establishing sure and permanent peace.
Examining the organization itself, one must, I think, readily assent to the view that the form of the organization in the field assigned to it is or promises to be satisfactory. It is modelled on a form which has been given to other international organizations established within the past year. It has a general conference, which corresponds to the assembly in the case of the united nations organization, and it has an executive board of eighteen and a permanent secretariat. There is a feature in connection with the organization which I think is worthy of mention. It will come into existence when twenty signatory nations ratify the constitution. The admission of members is put on this basis, that members of the united nations organization are automatically entitled to membership in UNESCO; and as to other nations which are not members of the united nations organization, they may be admitted by a two-thirds majority vote of the general conference. That will take care of any nations which are not yet signatories of the charter of the united nations organization.
As to the executive board, it is worthy of note that whereas membership in the general conference is on the basis of nations, when the selection is made of the eighteen members to constitute the general conference, they are selected as persons. There is one qualification in the agreement, to this effect, that no nation may have more than one representative on the executive board except in the case of the nation from which the president of the board is drawn.
The form of the organization promises, I believe, to be satisfactory. What shall we say of the purposes which have been assigned to it? On reading the purposes which have motivated the forty-four nations to sit down together and write this charter, one can say only that they have conceived the purpose of UNESCO in the loftiest terms. They have gone to some of the ultimate causes of war. They have opened with the challenging statement that, "since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed"; and in the succeeding statements in reference to the purposes there are certain expressions which ought to be set beside one another by way of contrast. On the one hand we have reference to suspicion and mistrust, the doctrine of the inequality of men and races, as being sources or breeders of
war and the spirit of war. On the other hand we have offered, as antidotes, the democratic principles of the dignity, equality and mutual respect of men, the wide diffusion of culture, the education of humanity for justice and liberty and peace, and finally, the intellectual and moral solidarity of mankind.
