speechtext:
Prior to the one o'clock adjournment I had touched on two of what I conceive to be three important matters affecting the resolution now before the house The first was the .form of organization of the united nations educational, scientific, and cultural organization. The second had to do with its purposes. I should like to read one further passage from the provisions setting forth the general objectives:-
For these reasons, the states parties to this constitution, believing in full and equal opportunities for education for all, in the unrestricted pursuit of objective truth, and in the free exchange of ideas and knowledge, are agreed and determined to develop and to increase the means of communication between their peoples and to employ these means for the purposes of mutual understanding and a truer and more perfect knowledge of each other's lives.
If I may interject there, that statement may appear to be a stumbling block to Russian participation in the UNESCO as constituted at present, because undoubtedly we have no evidence of a free exchange of ideas and knowledge being permitted by the Russian government with people in other parts of the world, or any willingness to increase the means of communication between their people and the other peoples of the world. If the time comes when that barrier is broken down and an exchange of information, ideas and understandings is permitted between the peoples of that country and the peoples of the rest of the world, then indeed we shall have achieved a greater measure of assurance of lasting peace.
Article I of this constitution has this to say:
The purpose of the organization is to contribute to peace and security by promoting among the nations through education, science and culture in order to further universal respect of justice, for the rule of law and for the human rights and fundamental freedoms which are affirmed for the peoples of the world, without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, by the Charter of the United Nations.
There we have a lofty statement of the purposes of this organization, a statement which must have the willing and enthusiastic
United Nations-Education

adherence of all enlightened peoples the world over. But, Mr. Speaker, we can have the most perfect form of organization, we can have the loftiest form of statement of the purposes of the organization, and yet see it waste, atrophy and fail. There is one factor which must be added to these two if this organization is to achieve for humanity the objects which it has set before it. That third factor is the will on the part of the governments of the states concerned, yes, and, beyond them, of the peoples in those states, to make this organization really effective for the achievement of the purposes set forth in the constitution. Unless that is made the real purpose on the part of the peoples of the world, and through them of their governments, this constitution will become but a musty document in the Canadian archives. It is a duty which rests on parliament, it is a duty which rests on the people in public life in this country and in other lands, to bring home to the people the fact that this organization is not far removed from contact with reality, that it is not something far removed from their experiences, but something which is vital to them in their hopes for lasting peace and an opportunity to live their lives in security.
What we need is a happy blend of idealism and realism. There will be some who will ask what immediate advantage this offers to Canada, and who will judge Canada's or this parliament's duty of adherence to this organization by the answer to that question. I do not believe any one of us can pretend that this organization offers some immediate special advantage to Canada. If we are to measure our efforts to build lasting peace simply by their immediate fruits, then I am afraid our measures are going to appear very ineffective indeed. We must take a long-range view and measure our progress in relation to long-range objectives.
I affirm with confidence that there is no nation, the world over, which has a greater stake in the peace of the world than has Canada. All of us are well aware of and conscious of the danger that if there should be another world war Canada may well be the battleground. We know that if we are to have hope of progressing and developing this land with all its great natural resources we must have peace and settled international relations. We know all too well the threat to national unity in this country which war has always brought. Therefore I say that this nation has as great a stake in international peace as any nation in the world.
There are some who will say, let us mind our own affairs, the education of our own

people, and let other people look after their own affairs. Are there any who say that in the light of the experience of the world in recent years? If there are, let them cast their minds back to what happened in Germany when Hitler came to power. Almost the first things he did were to abolish trade unions and to seize control of education. What happened? Hon. members well know the way that the educational system of that country was made to serve the purposes of the nazi ideology. Hon. members will recall the way in which the universities were closed, the libraries burnt, the university professors and teachers who were not prepared to inculcate the nazi ideology sent to the concentration camps, and the educational system bent to serve the purposes of the nazis. You remember, Mr. Speaker, that it was not a generation which was uneducated which burst forth upon the world in 1939, but a generation which was educated according to Nazi standards, a generation which like its fathers in 1914 thought that it was carrying a superior brand of culture to inferior peoples elsewhere in Europe and abroad. Yes, Mr. Speaker, you will recall the tramp, tramp of these booted nazi youths marching through Nuremburg in torchlight processions in the early days of the nazi regime shouting out, "Deutschland erwache"! Germany awake! And Germany awoke.
You remember also what happened to the educational institutions in the lands which were Subjugated by the nazis. They were among the first things of which the invaders seized control. They closed the educational institutions or used them to serve the nazi purposes. Anyone who dares to say that the education of the youth of other lands is no concern of Canada while we are training our youth for peace has closed his eyes to what has taken place. While we are training our youth for peace dare we shut our eyes if other nations are training th' ir youth for war? I say, no.
Consider the need in Europe to-day. The need is simply appalling. How can we expect any reconstruction of Europe, any return of Europe to peaceful objectives, unless there is a return of the educational and cultural institutions of that continent? It is good, Mr. Speaker, that the preparatory commission should have set this out as one of its first objectives. It will be found in article 6 of the instrument establishing the commission, as follows:
The commission shall appoint a special technical subcommittee to examine the problems relating to the educational, scientific and cultural needs of the countries devastated by the war, having regard to the information already collected and the work being done by other

United Nations-Education
international organizations, and to prepare as complete a conspectus as possible of the extent and nature of the problems for the information of the Organization at the First Session of the Conference.
We Canadians pride ourselves, and rightly, Mr. Speaker, on the contribution this country made to the winning of the war and to humanity through other media such as UNRRA and international loans. What we need to do now is to match that contribution with our contribution to mankind in the educational, scientific and cultural realm. In the educational realm no land in the world attaches greater importance to education than this country; in no land the world over, I suggest. is there a firmer conviction that the opportunities of education must be open to all on an equal footing, and in no country in the world is there a more determined attempt constantly to improve the methods of education. Furthermore, we have happily developed in this country a large number of educationists, leaders in that field, who with this widened opportunity are now capable of making a valued contribution in this realm to other lands as well.
In the field of science this country already possesses a formidable roll of great Canadians who have made vast contributions-and this is a matter of which I think Canadians should be especially proud-on the constructive side of science. Look at the list of the great Canadian scientists, and with very few exceptions .you will see that their contribution has been to the welfare of humanity rather than to developing means of destroying humanity.
In the third place, in regard to the cultural realm, I contend that this country is in a position to make a unique contribution. We have two great cultures in this country, to which have been added the cultures brought to this country by those whom we call new Canadians. We have flourishing here not only' the art, literature, music and humanities imported from other lands; we are also developing original accomplishments in these fields. This nation can measure its greatness and its accomplishments not simply in material things, but also in these things of the spirit.
Yes; we can contribute much to and we can receive much from this organization. It is worthy of note that already UNESCO has received the approbation of distinguished Canadians who are particularly concerned in this field. I quote only one such expression, contained in a newspaper interview given by Doctor Sidney Smith, president of the University of Toronto, appearing in the Globe and Mail of November 23 last. Speaking of UNESCO he said:
This new organ is as essential a prop to world security as any other agency in the united nations organization, economic, political or military.
Then he went on to observe, and I think this is worthy of note, that there was no comparable organization under the old league of nations.

The Secretary of State is quite right in referring to the organization for intellectual cooperation, but I suggest to the house that the aims of that organization were never carried to the length that has been outlined in the charter of the organization now before us.
Let us not forget' that we are not doing something light here to-day in approving this charter. Let us remember that we are assuming obligations. It is obvious that in the first place we have assumed an obligation in the field of education, science and culture, to try to mould our national objectives so they will be in harmony with those set forth in the constitution of UNESCO. That should not be difficult, because our aims in these fields are and always have been peaceful. But we must bear in mind also that there is a further step to be taken in the way of organization. In article YII of the charter we have this provision:
Each member state shall make such arrangements as suit its particular conditions for the purpose of associating its principal bodies interested in educational, scientific and cultural matters with the work of the organization, preferably by the formation of a national commission broadly representative of the government and such bodies.
I do not need to say more than a word on the subject of a national commission for Canada, in view of the remarks made this morning by the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), but I do offer two observations by way of caution. In the first place, if we are to have a national commission, as I hope we shall, it must be broad and representative in its composition- representative of the best Canadian thought and culture in these kindred fields of education, science and culture. In the second place, we must be very careful that we do not in any way interfere with or trespass upon the autonomy of the provinces in the matter of education. I am sure the house welcomed the assurance given this morning by the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs that no move will be made in this direction without full consultation with the provinces.
United Nations-Education

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that Canada's place is definitely in this organization, and that Canada must take a prominent, yes, a leading part in the functioning of the organization. We have in this country men of the calibre required to make the executive board of UNESCO a useful and outstanding organization. We have in this country men capable of making a great contribution to the deliberations of the general conference. Because of the part Canada played in the drafting of those provisions in the united nations charter which govern the powers, functions and purposes of the economic and social council, we shall wish to see to it that in UNESCO, so closely related in its objects to the economic and social council, the work is carried forward in complete loyalty to its stated objectives.
It would be a brave man indeed, perhaps only a foolhardy one, who would prophesy success for this organization. It may be difficult for many to see an assurance of success for it until Russia participates and cooperates fully. But the possibility of Russia still standing aside and declining to cooperate or participate, in my humble submission, still is not the greatest danger to the success of the organization. The greatest danger wall be the indifference and apathy of governments, of parliaments and of peoples, the feeling that this sort of organization is altogether too remote from them. The greatest danger will be that parliaments, perhaps this one this afternoon, will say, "When we have ratified this charter we have done all that is expected of us." In ratifying this charter, as I trust parliament will ratify it, we are not fulfilling our obligation. We are rather assuming and acknowledging an obligation which must be fulfilled over the years to come. It is needful for us to realize that to-day we are simply taking the first step, that we are accepting an obligation. Its fulfilment in the years to come will be a high privilege and a great responsibility for all men in public life in this country.

You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that I listened with great interest to the address of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). You may be sure that I am very much interested in the resolution, such as it is, presented by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this morning, and a little later I shall try to explain what I mean by "such as it is." I was interested in hearing the preamble read; I believe it included some such words as "it is in the minds of men that wars begin. It is in the minds of men that understanding must be created." Whether or not the first part

of that paragraph is true, I shall not discuss here. I could debate it, I think, at some length. But I do certainly believe it is in the minds of men that understanding must be created.
May I say I was somewhat disappointed in the comments made this morning by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), because I felt he was expressing a narrow nationalist point of view. I believe we should share in common with all the people of the world, whether it be in health matters or matters of education, all such knowledge as we have been fortunate enough to get into our possession.
I should like to congratidate the minister upon bringing in this resolution. Many of us have been waiting for it, and for more, for a long time. It will be welcomed throughout the whole country by those who are interested in education.

In view of the activities of the preparatory committee which has been meeting in London recently,^ and in view of the way their action may easily affect Canada, we are very anxious that the Canadian parliament should ratify the UNESCO charter and should set up the enabling bodies which would act with the commissioners, or representatives, who would represent Canada on the UNESCO council. 1.	Each member state shall make such arrangements as suit its particular conditions for the purpose of associating its principal bodies interested in educational, scientific and cultural matters with the work of the organization, preferably by the formation of a national commission broadly representative of the government and such bodies.

to the general conference and to their governments in matters relating to the organization and shall function as agencies of liaison in all matters of interest to it.

In the budget debate I had urged that upon the minister, when I said:
I urge upon the government some immediate action by way of a beginning. In this field there is no minister, no government department to give a lead; some leadership should be arranged forthwith.

This body fills an absolute need. As I pointed out, there is no minister, and no department. How can such a body be made up? Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the constitution of this organization. As hon. members know, it was the United States which proposed the San Francisco conference. Russia was against it; Churchill was against it. However it was the idea of the late president of the United States, who did so much for civilization. What happened? The big powers were unrepresented except by members of the cabinet; the leaders were not there. They inserted in the charter of the united nations a veto clause for the big four. Here you have Russia, the United States and Great Britain, and now they have added China and France. They divided the world into large powers, the big five; middle powers and smaller nations. As you know, the whole proceeding down there at San Francisco for security has collapsed, after Moscow, Potsdam, Yalta and Paris. There is no such thing in the world to-day as collective security. When you read over this document, treaty series No. 18, final act, you find on page 32 a list of the big four, the middle powers and the smaller nations. You find also that to-day almost every one of them is violating the world's charter which was drawn up at San Francisco. It has turned out to be nothing but a scrap of paper. If we are to have all this internationalism we will lead the countries to another war. Let us start our internationalism with the British
United Nations-Education

empire first. I should like to read two or three quotations from the constitution, the first being:
-that since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.
Those are not original words; they are copied from the theory of Abbe de St. Pierre, who first set these words out in his "Theory (1713) of Collective Security". The main object of this new organization is to change the hearts of men. As I pointed out, a great historian, Professor S. R. Gardiner, commenting on the treaty of Utrecht of 1713, said:
The truth is that states combine readily through fear and very seldom through a desire for the common good, and when Louis XIV ceased to be formidable, each state thought exclusively of its own interests.
That is what each of the smaller and middle states are doing to-day, and the larger powers too. What happened last November when this organization was meeting in London? The big powers had a conference at Moscow and at Yalta. What happened over there? Mr. Attlee was there, Mr. Bevin was there, Mr. Byrnes and Mr. Stalin were there at Moscow. What did they do? They carved up Europe and the result is that the twenty-one nations who met at San Francisco, now at Paris, have no more to do than the man in the moon with the peace division of Europe, because one of the large powers can veto everything they do. The whole organization at San Francisco fell to the ground by this absurd veto insertion, because any one of the big powers can veto all the acts of the others.
What about this change in the hearts of men? No one sees it as yet after 150 years since Abbe de St. Pierre's days. I quote from page 10 of the final act, treaty series 1945, No. 18 united nations conference to establish security, as follows:

that ignorance of each other's ways and lives has been a common cause, throughout the history of mankind, of that suspicion and mistrust between the peoples of the world through which their differences have all too often broken into war;
that the great and terrible war which has now ended was a war made possible by the denial of the democratic principles of the dignity, equality and mutual respect of men, and by the propagation, in their place, through ignorance and prejudice, of the doctrine of the inequality of men and races.
What has been the result of all that? They simply copied the language which was used after the battle of Waterloo in the Concert of Europe when there was talk again about changing the hearts of men. In 1713 the great learned French scholar, Abbe de St. Pierre, first set out the theory of collective security in France. He went to a very able cardinal of
rMr. Church.]
France, Cardinal Fleury, and asked him to consider the scheme. The cardinal replied, "Have you sent out missionaries to turn the hearts of men?" That is what should have been done down in San Francisco. Instead of sending delegates from Canada and the other countries we should have sent missionaries down there to change the hearts of men. Until the hearts of men are changed there will be war as long as time lasts. Nearly seventy-five or eighty years ago Ruskin, one of the greatest authors of his day, and a man of peace, spoken of war; he said exactly what the cardinal said in "His Crown of Olives," to show the folly of all this new form of pacifism.
They had the Concert of Europe after the war of 1815 which was set up along the same lines as this organization, to change the hearts of men for scientific and educational purposes and for the good of humanity. The very same language was used then when they set up the Concert of Europe, composed of Austria, Prussia and Russia, after the battle of Waterloo. Nothing more was heard of collective security until by this new pact made in 1815 Emperor Alexander I of Russia proposed what is known as the Holy Alliance, or the Concert of Europe. Between whom? Between Austria, Prussia and Russia. They were to meet every few years, the contracting parties, to look over the face of Europe and see how peace and security was. What didi it lead to? It led to the great prime minister of Great Britain. George Canning, urging that Britain should get out of Europe and seek a new alliance for a while; and it led by provocation to the United States adopting the Monroe doctrine in 1823. As Lord Castlereagh, the great British foreign minister, wrote to Lord Liverpool in 1815 at the Quai d'Orsay, "It was not without difficulty that we went through the interview with becoming gravity." It was the spiritual force between the Concert of Europe of which Russia, Austria and Prussia were *the protagonists. They were the high contracting parties. It lasted eight years, its most notable achievement being that it provoked the United States into establishing the Monroe doctrine in 1823.
Then followed1 over a century or more, more security pacts in Dumbarton Oaks and the San Francisco conference. But what does it lead to? The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) seems to have great faith in this new pacifist organization, but I have none at all. As has been said, Russia has a treaty with Great Britain for ten years, and France and Britain must have a treaty or understanding immediately if they are to preserve any security for the world on the western front in the future. Unless we can continue the coopera-

United Nations-Education
tion that existed during the war between Russia and the United States and Great Britain, then all collective security will be at an end.
What nations were represented at London on November 16, 1945? I will name just two, Greece and Turkey. Greece was against us in the first world war, and so was Turkey. What are they doing to-day? In view of Great Britain abandoning the Suez canal they were said to be trying actively to get an arrangement with Russia behind the scenes. So are several of the other nations seeking alliances, defensive and offensive. The great and small nations are seeking alliances with each other because they feel that only by having alliances can they keep the peace and security part of this organization. Without that, the educational, cultural and scientific oarts of it will come to an end.
There is nothing said in this pact about cooperation and coordination in connection with the atomic bomb. The only league of nations that ever was a success to carry out educational, scientific and cultural work was the British empire. That is the only successful league of nations we have ever had1.
On page 4 of the final act it states:
The following international organizations were also represented by observers:
International labour organization.
That has very little to do with this organization's function, as it is simply done for labour by another organization for labour. Talk about the league of nations and security -it was the league of nations that caused the second W'orld war. It was nothing but pure sham and humbug of the league that led to the second world war. It was the league of nations that led Britain and the United States to disarm. It led Britain to throw away the finest navy, the finest army and the finest air force the world had ever seen, and allowed Hitler to rearm and scrap the Versailles treaty. It led to the second1 world war. And now they are at it again, these pacifist leagues! They have formed a new league organization with a new name and are appearing before even our own external affairs committee. I see represented at London last November the PanAmerican union. We are a member of the British empire. The greatest league of nations that the wmrld ever knew was the British empire; Great Britain and the commonwealth and the dominions, all united together are the hope for peace and for the defence of the world. Britain and the commonwealth had to go it alone in the early years of the war. Russia at that time had a treaty and an alliance with Germany, and for two years she stayed on Germany's side. Then Russia violated her treaty and came over to us. Russia might have lost the war but for Britain and the commonwealth alone for two years fighting Germany.
I say that this sort of organization has been tried before and it has failed for over two centuries. So far as science goes, there may be something in that. I referred to science and the part it has played when the minister's estimates were up last year. I said:
Take modern medicine alone, the child of science, the most promising and brightest-eyed of her family. If it has not mastered, it has so diminished as to rob bodily pain of its terrors.
That is true. But science does not need the help of any pacifist paper organization like this. We have seen what happened about the atomic bomb. Science can get very little help from a paper organization like this, which will lead only to war instead of bringing about peace and security.
Bishop Rennison in one of his articles referred to the tower of Babel and said that we have another tower of Babel in San Francisco, Yalta and others of these pacts which are being made among the nations of the world to-day. He said that they mean nothing unless first there is a change in the hearts of men and we go back to the principles of the original Christian church. Next to the Christian church the British empire has done most for peace and security. I have very little faith in these international bodies. We saw the result of their work in the first world war and between the two wars.
Some of the countries that are listed as members of this organization were on the side of Germany in the last war-Argentine and others listed now. Some of these pacifist organizations have caused disunity within the empire and the abandonment of the Suez canal, which is the jugular vein of the British empire. India is also listed at the back of the book. It is the lifeline of the British empire, just as preferential trade is the bloodstream of the British empire. Some of these countries here did nothing for us in the war at all, and here they are signing their names to the final act, to a paper pact that means nothing. If Canada joins this organization it will be just like the other league. Canada will pay just like she did before, while many of the twenty-one member countries never paid a cent of their allotted contributions to the old league. I would like to see this session closed at the end of next week, but I object to these matters being dealt with in this manner. It is impossible to discuss them properly at the resolution stage, and without their being referred to a committee.
United Nations-Education

I saw the first great war coming, and I was a lone voice in this house in urging preparations for it. I urged rearmament all along the line, and trade, defence and migration within the empire. I can tell you this, that a lot of these organizations are not worth a snap of the finger so. far as scientific or educational results are concerned for peace or security or anything else. Education is exclusively a provincial matter. In 1937 and 1938 and 1939 I told the pacifists in this house that war was coming and that we should rearm, but I was not heeded. Then the war came, and after the first world war the league of nations was established, and then we had a second world war, and we are heading into a third world war if we depend on pacifist organizations like this. While I am a strong supporter of science and education, I have very little faith in any of these organizations. The San Francisco conference took place eight months before a presidential election, and resulted in nothing but more chaos and confusion, and caused friction with Russia. What has Russia done? She has taken over Persia and captured the Balkans and Roumania. She has gone in there and established a system of communism in all the Balkan countries. She has got control of eastern and central Europe. I for one have no faith in organizations like this, or the new league of the same old source. I have read the debates in the British house on this proposal and I believe that men of science or educational authorities will have very little to do with this organization. I believe it will do nothing at all for education or science or to prevent war. Talk about pacifism -there are one or two organizations represented in this building to-day-labour and steel strike organizations. How are you going to pacify the world if you cannot pacify labour now in our building? How are you going to change the hearts of men? I was in Hamilton on Sunday and it is like an armed camp at the steel plant. Better start in at Ottawa changing the hearts of men in a domestic strike first. Then you may get somewhere. But these international paper organizations are nothing but a waste of public money.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider this one of the most important resolutions to come before the house. It is far-reaching and has great possibilities. I do not think everything that is written into this treaty or into the resolution can be accomplished immediately, but I am inclined to have a little more faith in the possibilities than some of the speakers from whom we have heard so far. If I were asked to summarize the purport of the whole thing 
in a slogan I would call it "Peace through education." The opening sentence of the preamble sums it up very well. The acting Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has referred to it already. It says that the defences of peace must be constructed in the minds of men.
I cannot agree with the whole sentence, because it says first of all that wars begin in the minds of men.. That is only relatively true. If we were to give it a very wide and general interpretation we might be able to say that that is true; but it fails, it seems to me, to take into consideration certain other causes which are far more important than the mere mental condition of the people. I have too much faith in humanity to believe that people declare war on each other or fight each other merely because they dislike each other. It is quite true that people who do fight must first dislike each other, but it seems to me that the root causes of war go much deeper than mere dislikes or hatreds that are the immediate point from which people begin to fight. I am inclined to think that there are certain considerations such as the following which have not been faced up to in this declaration.
For example, they do not seem to take into consideration the clash of economic interests. We must be realistic as well as idealistic,-to paraphrase what the hon. member to my right (Mr. Fleming) said'-and realize that so long as we talk in terms of international competition-and we had an example of that yesterday, listening to one of the speeches on export trade, about competing with our neighbour nations for the markets or the resources of the world-we are going in the direction of conflict. I think we must approach it from the point of view of cooperating with other nations in sharing the wealth of the world, realizing that we have now reached the point where it can be said definitely that there is enough for all. That may not have been true a hundred years ago. It certainly can be said to-day that, with the power of production which the world possesses, there is enough for all if it is shared in cooperation; but if it is put on the basis of competing for it, we shall do what we have done before, we shall waste and destroy it, and everyone will be hungry in the end.
Again, there is the consideration of the economic exploitation of man by man. This is a realistic consideration, and one which we must face. A moment ago the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) brought up that point in a different way when he remarked that one of the cities in this country has

United Nations-Education
reached a condition where it is practically an armed camp. Why? Is it because there is not enough food, clothing and shelter in this country to go round? Is it that they are fighting over something -which all cannot have? It is not that, but because there are in our economic system people-whom I do not blame individually, because they are the product of the system which has been built up-who have more economic power and have concentrated more wealth in their hands than they are willing to allow their fellow men to possess. That exploitation causes men to envy and hate each other and in the long run leads to conflict.
Then there is the contraction of the world community. We have good examples of that all around us. Every time we see the news on the screen we are struck by the fact that the world seems to be continually getting smaller. To-day distance does not count for what it did years ago; and the bringing together, sometimes the sudden bringing together, of the peoples of the world by our modern means of communication creates certain types of friction which must be overcome before we can say that "war begins in the minds of men."
Perhaps the greatest of all is the failure of nations so far to make adjustments in their social and economic philosophies and systems to keep up with the advance of science and with technological development. I do not think anyone will disagree when I say that socially and economically we have not kept up with the times. We have found it possible through scientific skill to develop certain processes and inventions and certain ways of doing things which were not dreamed of a century ago, but in our economic and social thinking we have not advanced at the same rate.
With that inf induction I want to say that I do have faith and hope that this organization will amount to something more than is possible at the present time. In article I, under the heading "Purposes and functions", we find something which it seems to me could have been more properly divided into three parts, because it sets out the purpose of the organization, the reason for those purposes, and also the method. For example, the purpose is, "to contribute to peace and security". There is no quarrel as 'o the desirability of that. The reason, it goes on to say, is "to further universal respect of justice, for the rule of law and for the human rights and fundamental freedoms which are affirmed for the peoples of the world, without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, by the charter of the united nations." Also very
desirable, very elevated. We come to the third part, the method by which this is to be attained, namely, "by promoting collaboration among the nations through education, science and culture." It is this part of article I which I want to question. I am not altogether sure that this constitution provides, or at any rate adequately provides, for that method, because if we turn to the third paragraph of article I we find this clause:
The organization is prohibited from intervening in matters which are essentially within their domestic jurisdiction.
I do not want it to appear as though I was in favour of interfering with anyone's domestic matters, whether provincial or national, but I do say that if we are to have education for peace, and if it is to be effective, it must be universal. I join with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in his deep regret that the Soviet union and the republics associated with it have not seen fit so far to become participants in this organization, because I believe that both the Soviet union and the countries which are now in the organization would gain much and lose nothing by standing together and working out ideas on world affairs. If education for peace is to be effective, it must be universal; it cannot be limited. We shall have to work towards that objective, because if we do not, I am afraid that what the hon. member for Broadview said will be only too true, that it will be a paper organization and nothing more.
What do I mean by "universal"? I do not mean that through the united nations organization full power and jurisdiction will be had over education in every school of the world, but that through that organization there must, be power to present at least a minimum programme. It would be by its nature very limited in scope, because it would have to be the most that all could agree upon, and that would be precious little at this time. But if we can find even a modicum of education for peace on which all nations can agree, and then give the united nations organization the power to see that this type of education is available in every school in the world, we shall have made a step towards peace. If we do not do that, I fear we shall not have accomplished anything.
Those who fear that this interference with the domestic education of nations will be a serious contravention of our sovereignty will find, if they turn to the powers given to the security council, that that council under the united nations organization is empowered to interfere physically in the affairs of nations
United Nations-Education

when there is a threat of war. Surely, by the same logic and reasoning, if it is necessary to give powers to the security council to interfere physically in the affairs of nations in order to avoid the threat of war, it is just as reasonable to say that we should give to UNESCO or the united nations enough power to lay the foundations of peace in the first place, in order that it may not be necessary for the security council to interfere with physical force in order to put down aggression when it has already raised its head. I think that is fundamental; and if we are going to get into this we might as well get into it and be serious about it. I would have no hesitation in giving UNESCO sufficient power to enable it to present a minimum .programme of education for peace in every school room of the world. A great deal more could be said about it, but most of these considerations have been pointed out by other hon. members.
Listening to the hon. member from Lethbridge I. could not help but agree with him to this extent, that if this organization is to be successful it must be practical and it must begin at home. Sometimes I am a little surprised at how quick and ready we are to sign our names to and endorse great and high sounding objectives provided it is something that we shall not have to do. It is not so long since I had the honour of introducing a resolution to provide for equality of education in Canada. I mention that merely because these very -words are used in one of the objectives of this organization; not for Canada only but for all the people of the world. Although my resolution received some sympathetic consideration on this side of the house, it was given none on the other side. I am a little concerned as to how we, who are not willing to extend equality of opportunity and education to our own citizens, are to undertake to do it for all the peoples of the world. I hope that we shall begin at home. But I do not agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge when he says that our philosophy has to be one of minding our own business. I have no objection to anyone minding his own business provided that we as a nation could mind our business within the borders of our own country. If that were possible I should be glad to follow his advice, but in our has to be one of minding our own business, seems to be scattered all over the world. The world seems to have arrived at the stage where you cannot draw a boundary line and say, up to here is indeed my business and from here on it is not. It simply does not work that way. We shall have to make up our minds whether we are going to cooperate with other nations in taking part in organizations of
 .
this kind, in the hope that through collective action we may preserve peace, or whether we are going to hide our heads in the sand in the hope that when the avalanche comes it will be outside our own particular area.

I shall not take more than just a few minutes of the time of the house. I really want to register my objection to certain phases of the agreement now before us.
Let me say at the outset that I am in hearty agreement with every move which will bring the nations together in cooperation to do anything which is necessary to be done for human good. I agree that a great deal may be accomplished by cooperation in the way of extending education, good will, science and so forth. To that extent I am in favour of the proposal now before us. But I think it is unfortunate that such good objectives should have been postulated on what is to me an absurdity and an error, an error biologically, historically, scientifically or in any way you wish to take it. And that error is the one upon which most hon. members who have supported this agreement have pinned their faith, namely, that since wars begin in the minds of men it is in the minds of men that the defence of peace must be constructed. I say that that is simply a false philosophy; it is an assertion for the truth of which there is no evidence in history or in science. Apparently it is only because we can swallow that error that this parliament and this nation and others can proceed with policies which are fast developing the next war, while we indulge in verbal effusions of this kind about trying to prevent it.
So long as struggle is the means by which men and nations exist, nations will fight. The human family had been fighting for millions of years before it had any mind at all-some of them have not very much yet-and to assume that it was their minds which made them fight is nothing but an absurdity. I think it is just hypocritical for us to hold to lofty verbal peace objectives, as we are doing here if we subscribe to this agreement, while we have already committed this nation to the conflict method of existence. To-day this nation stands for free private enterprise, which is the conflict system, the tooth and claw method, the struggle for existence, the mere animalism and junglism of history.

My hon. friend has not got out of it yet. We have committed ourselves to that. That is what this nation stands for, and if every other nation stands for it there

United Nations-Education
is going to be conflict. I do not care what kind of minds people have, nor do I care what is in them, if there is a scarcity of anything in any nation in a world of conflict, where only by conflict they can exist, then war will most certainly come. Therefore the very basis of any hope of the future peace of the world must be in so arranging the essentials of our human life on a cooperative basis that man will be able to live without killing somebody else in order to do it. No amount of education, whatever that education may be, will remove the facts. You may educate this nation, if that be possible, to believe that the stars began in the human mind, that the moon is merely the creation of the human mind, and then say if you could abolish that idea in the human mind you would abolish the moon and the stars; but you will not. It may be possible to induce the human mind to think it is just man's mind that wants to fight and make war. No doubt the desire to fight can be stimulated by education when the cause for war is already operating, but if the real cause is not there, then man will not fight..
The only alternative to a conflict economy is a cooperative economy, and that is the thing which is lacking. It has been deplored that Russia has not joined this organization. There is enough nonsense in the first sentence to prevent Russia from joining, and it should prevent us from joining if it was taken seriously, which I hope we shall not do.
If we are to further education and science in the international field, we must do more than merely pass resolutions. I have already pointed out what is to me a hypocritical position when we further an economy which makes war inevitable and pass or endorse agreements which stand for the abolition of it. Education, scientific research and so forth have values, great values and they, as I said at the outset, may be furthered by international action. To the extent that they may be furthered I am for this agreement. But there is no use in passing this even for that purpose unless the government will commit itself to carry out its share of the bargain. That means it has to set up the machinery necessary to further education and science on the international plane. So far as I can recall, in his remarks the minister did not commit the government to the immediate carrying out of articles 4 and 8 of the agreement, for instance, as we have them here. Unless that is done, nothing will be done. Article 4 provides:
The general conference shall consist of the representatives of the states members of the organization. The government of each member state shall appoint not more than five delegates,
who shall be selected after consultation with the national commission, if established, or with educational, scientific, and cultural bodies.
I should like to press the minister to give this parliament the assurance that on the endorsation of this document the government will take the necessary steps immediately to fulfil its obligations as contained in article 4, and carry them out according to articles 7 and 8.

speechtext:
I was very much interested in the references to the preamble of the constitution, by the last two speakers in particular, who took some exception to it. They devoted considerable time-* and perhaps they are right-in, an endeavour to refute the argument that "since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed". I was a little surprised to find that some of the arguments against the inclusion of that language, to which I think one hon. gentleman referred as nonsense, came from a speech of the socialist Prime Minister of Great Britain, who in the course of his remarks at the plenary session of the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization used exactly those words: "Wars begin in the minds of men." Apparently the influence of the Prime Minister of Great Britain was felt so strongly at the meeting which finally drew up the constitution that those words were placed in the very beginning of the preamble to which hon. gentlemen to my left have taken exception. I am not in a position particularly to discuss that aspect of it, but I thought perhaps this should be put on the record to show there are divergent views with respect to the matter.
I want to point out just one or two things in connection with the constitution that is before us, and one thing that strikes me as being perhaps the weak link in the whole UNESCO structure. That is the fact that three very important and powerful members of the united nations not only did not participate in the final signing of the constitution, as hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house have pointed out, but as far as my information goes did not even accept the invitation to attend the meetings of the united nations conference for the establishment of an educational, scientific and cultural organization. Those three nations are the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the Ukraine and ByeloRussia.
Whatever may be said with respect to the necessity for organizations of this kind, I do not rise this afternoon for the purpose of
United Nations-Education

throwing cold water upon any plan which in the final analysis may make some contribution to world peace and international security. I take the view that as a Canadian parliament we cannot put ourselves in the position of placing obstacles in the way of {setter international understanding. It may be that many of these organizations have their weaknesses. I believe they have, and I think that is so right fom the top international organization down to and including some of its lesser component parts. Nevertheless we have to consider international problems from a much wider viewpoint. I have always felt, and I think it is the opinion of this house, that San Francisco, the general assembly, the security council, the economic and social council and the other organizations connected with UNO at least go this far; at least they provide a table under which the nations of the world may put their fact and talk things over instead of shouldering rifles and going to war to fight it out. Surely that is a factor we must not overlook in deciding whether to play our part in the various organizations set up for the purpose of achieving the objective of international peace and security. While this organization itself has obvious weaknesses, nevertheless I think we can still say it is a step in the right direction, even if it is but a halting step; and we must take that halting step in the interests of world peace.
One of the problems the nations of the world face to-day is that of seeing that the major powers, particularly, find some basis for collaboration. It is not enough to bring together dozens of little powers throughout the world and have them collaborate. They all have their Tights, and no one would be more anxious to champion those rights than I. But when one appreciates that something over eighty-five per cent of the war potential of the world, the power to wage war, rests in the hands of three nations, then I think one gets the picture in proper perspective and sees what we have to do in order to achieve a system of world security for the days that lie ahead. The weakness of this organization will 'be admitted, I am sure, even by those who are its greatest proponents and. advocates. When one of those three great powers is out of the organization, together with two republics which are within its geographical boundary, we start this race with only one leg, and we have something less than a proper launching of an organization of the kind. I think the weakness of the old league of nations arose from a similar situation, because one of the great powers was unable to see its way clear to play the full part it normally would play in

any great association of powers. But in any of these organizations where one of the major powers decides to stay out, and not only does not sign but does not attend and does not subscribe to the purposes and objectives of the organization, it will be seen at once where the weakness of such organizations must lie.
One of the great means of education in the world to-day is the press. Whatever weaknesses some people may think it has, let me say that without a free press throughout the world it is difficult to have democracy functioning as it should. If we were to take the free press from Canada, inside of six months we would not have an effective democratic system functioning. Those avenues for the dissemination of information, the press and the radio, and other means of communication, are the means of keeping together the thoughts of the people of our nation, and of correlating their efforts with those who sit in parliaments or on other representative bodies. I think there is little use at the moment in holding out more than the laudable objective of world government. I am one who hopes it may come. But I believe the basis of it must be laid on the foundation of a free and untrammelled press and radio throughout the world. These are the important components in the success of any kind of government; surely we cannot afford to ignore them in the formation of a world government.
In UNESCO we find a move to correlate, even to form a clearing house for and to advance and promote where we can, the educational, scientific and cultural talents of various nations. It is an effort to make a world in which we can live as good neighbours, and a medium through which we can impart to our neighbours any influence we may have or contribution we can make in these fields, while at the same time receiving from them the advantage of types of education and other knowledge more familiar to them.
The weakness of the organization in my view-and I am sure the minister will be the first to agree with me-is that for some reason, whatever it may be, a great and major power in the world has seen fit not to endorse the principle of or to participate in the UNESCO organization.
In our approach to international problems I believe our people ought to understand that we should not place these new organizations and new movements on a pedestal so high that, once these agreements are on paper, the people may think that peace has been achieved once and for all. The objectives of peace are not achieved simply by what is written on

United, Nations-Education
paper. The answer to this is found in what the great powers will do in relation to this subject. The answer to peace or war depends largely, if not altogether, not necessarily upon the education of the w'orld at large, but rather upon the ability and capacity and willingness -this last being the most important-of the three major powers to get along together in peace and harmony in the days which lie ahead. That, in a nutshell, is the problem of world peace. It seems to me we can put it boldly and concisely by saying that if the big powers stick together we shall have peace and, conversely, if they do not, anything may happen.
This is why I have risen this afternoon to say a word about this organization which does not embrace all of the three powers to which I have referred. I support the position taken by the government in asking parliament to accept the constitution. I believe it is a step in the right direction, but at the same time I am pointing out the definite weaknesses inherent in that constitution.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended saying anything, but I am moved to do so from what I have heard in the last half-hour I have been in the house.
This resolution deals with the establishment of an educational, scientific and cultural organization. I ask myself this question: to what example of the past are we to look for future educational, scientific and cultural standards? Are we to take the so-called education which in fact has been pure propaganda not only in this country but in Great Britain and the United States? Is the propaganda which has poured from the United States in the last several years to be the basis of the world's cultural education?
Who is to say what the world is to be taught? In this connection I would refer to a man whose name has been mentioned recently in the house. I refer to Doctor Chisholm, who has publicly denied the existence of right and wrong, who has openly sneered at Christianity and particularly at our Christmas. Having done that he is considered a great man and has been given one of the leading positions in a world organization. I wonder if he had sneered at a religious festival such as the Passover whether he would have been given that world job. I rather think not. There would have been no reward for him then. Evidently, however, he knew that a passport to one of these world jobs is to sneer at Christianity. That seems to be the fashion these days, and if one does not do it one is either a fascist or anti-Semitic.
In the matter of bringing peace through the united nations, only yesterday I referred to the treatment of Argentina at San Francisco. Was that the way to promote peace in the world? I was glad to hear the Speaker read out a message of felicitation from the Argentine parliament a few minutes after I made that protest, and we replied to it in like manner.	,
Then there is Spain. The very people who are behind all this international stuff are those who are demanding another civil war in Spain. For what purpose? To tear down one dictator in order to set up another. There is no suggestion that the Spanish people should be allowed to choose their own government. The whole agitation behind this promotion of another war in Spain is communistic, and nothing else.

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) asked me a question with regard to the export of flour from Lethbridge, Alberta, to Ecuador, and I told him I would give him an answer later.
Canada has a number of flour markets which she has traditionally served. Ecuador is one. In 1935 we shipped 12,773 barrels; in 1936, 17,511 barrels, and in 1937, 10,431 barrels. In keeping with the general policy of sending as much foodstuffs as possible to the United Kingdom, UNRRA, and the distressed areas, shipments to other markets have been drastically reduced. Thus, in 1945 we shipped only 5,597 barrels to Ecuador and shipments so far this year have been at approximately the same rate. The aggregate of shipments to South and Central America is insignificant in relation to the total wheat and flour production; but distribution to a few old customers and some new ones, it is hoped, will make possible the holding of existing markets and gaining a small foothold in some new ones that will be of inestimable value to the whole of Canada in the future. Furthermore, if we were to stop shipments altogether, the people of Ecuador would simply be driven to other sources of supply-it would not increase the world supply-and Canada would simply be taking on a larger share of relief shipments, while other countries took the commercial business that has future prospects.
Personally I welcome the information that Alberta mills are getting into this new export field.

speechtext:
As a real public ownership man the bill is a surprise to me in some ways. The Canadian National railway organization represents a consolidation of a number of systems, subsidiaries and other agencies on land, on the sea and in the air, and the hotel system. Many other subsidiaries were consolidated. In reality the system was not a real public ownership organization. It was founded on the mistakes made all over the country by private ownership in a financial way and the road was taken over by the government. There was a survey made and a report on railways brought forward in 1917 by the Drayton-Acworth report-regarding a method of financing the system, and as to guarantees which have become fabulous and a heavy drain on the country in the way of federal subsidies. The survey was made in 1917, and the Drayton-Acworth report issued on over capitalization of 40,000 miles of single track roads of this system and also 42,000 miles of single track roads of the other efficient privately owned system. The heavy overcapitalization laid a severe debt for the Canadian National on this country. Then the former separate Canadian National parts came to the provinces with this method of financing of capital and asked for guarantees from the provinces. Sections 1 and 2 should be taken together since they are both the same thing.
I wish to point out that some of these old securities go back to 1931. The marginal notes and headlines are part of the bill. You have to read the marginal notes as well as the headlines and sections of the bill. The second section of the bill refers to $7,000,000 for acquisition of the Manitoba railway. That road is as old as the hills. Then there is a section which gives the Minister of Finance power to make temporary loans, such as notes, bonds, loans, debentures, for capital expenditures, in regard to current indebtedness. In my opinion, such finance has been attacked severely in the report to which I refer. The present company has done well during the war. It gave good service, but the employees are not treated in the way that they should be. You and I, Mr. Chairman, travel on the system, and we know that some of these old, reliable employees have to work sixteen, seventeen and eighteen hours a day, moving from

Halifax the forces returning home from Europe. They should receive a bonus or some allowance for war work. It is not ownership such as the provincial hydro and the municipal hydro systems which treat their employees in a fair way for overtime and give them better labour conditions, such as train crews should have in demobilization.
This bill should have been considered by the select committee on railway and shipping or by some other committee on finances. It is a legal bill as well. Bill No. 346 consolidates the method of financing and it refers to $22,000,000. This amount should have been paid out of earnings. In a system like this, some provision should be made for paying out of earnings a lot of this for operating renewals on terminals, equipment, overhauling of cars and things of that kind, of a temporary and permanent nature not suitable for capital charges. That might have been provided out of earnings. The trouble with the system is that we have a lot of directors who do not direct, and some of them have no knowledge of railways or their operation. They are selected as directors for geographical and political reasons and not for public ownership reasons. There is no public ownership man I know of, connected with the road. I have supported this principle for many, many years. First of all, they moved their offices to Montreal. Ontario was the public ownership province. That is where the consolidated road made most of its earnings. We have very little to say in it at all. Then there is an additional amount asked for additions and betterments, retirement of maturing capital obligations and so forth. There is an item of $8,000,000 for new equipment. Very little of that comes to Canada. The United States affiliations are getting it, or most of it. A curious thing is that the United States affiliations and subsidiaries of this system are phenomenal for new equipment and betterments; they are almost equal to the system in the empire state express trains. During the war they did not get much out of the old chair system of better cars by day, all reserved for a small charge. You could travel on the American railway system thus during the war. If so, in Canada, you could have travelled on the three or four o'clock train for Montreal or Ottawa where they used to run chair cars, but they did not have any in war time, with the result that the trains were crowded.
There are many other matters that I should like to discuss, but I have just about finished. In my opinion the method of financing is all wrong. More should be paid for out of

income. The auditor general, and not just a private auditor, should have some control over the system. I have no doubt that better work would be thus done by the auditor general. All kinds of commissions are appointed, but during the session we have no control over them. Then, references are made to the committee and nobody can ask any questions about it. In the dying days of parliament we get this bill or a report of a committee on this great national system on which this country has spent hundreds of millions of dollars, on land and sea, in the air, and the hotel system at large, and we have no control over it. In my opinion we need a revision of our rules. I have read the reports of the railways and shipping committee. They smoke good cigars there, no doubt, and ask many questions, but it is no proper review of such a vast enterprise. The very first thing is a proper examination of the budget of hundreds of millions of dollars of this system and all its branches. No department or business would think of doing business with only a cursory examination by a select committee. I compliment the young minister because he has shown a great deal of zeal, and courtesy to private members and others, and he is always willing to answer letters or questions and give any information he can; but I wish to point out to him that Ontario, where they are making most of the revenue, is not getting its fair share of the betterments, equipment and the other matters regarding refinancing. Section 2 refers to $17,500,000 available from reserves for depreciation and debt discount amortization. Then there is $7,000,000 for the acquisition of the Manitoba railway. You will find, refunding bonds on a dollar parity, will cause trouble, and you will experience a lot of difficulty in that connection. This is not a very good time to go into the United States market. I believe if we had some other system of financing and more betterments out of revenue the people would get better value for their money. I travel on the trains and I tell the committee that the rolling stock and equipment in Ontario could be improved.
We want a real public ownership system for that public ownership province. I believe that the minister has been giving public ownership a fair trial since he has been in the department. I do say that more money should be paid out of earnings for all these minor repairs and maintenance charges. A lot of it could be paid out of earnings instead of its being charged up to capital, making vast refunding necessary.

subtopic: REENACTMENT OP REGULATIONS MADE BY ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the discussion that took place previously with respect to this bill, nor am I aware whether any detailed explanation has been given as to its purposes, objects and so on. At this stage, however, perhaps the minister might give a comprehensive review of the circumstances that led up to the necessity of having this measure, brought in, and also what the measure proposes to do.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This matter was fully gone into by the committee on external affairs. The statement made there, which I shall briefly repeat here, was along the following lines.
It was felt that His Excellency the Governor General, as commander in chief of the Canadian armies, has the right to take such measures for the conduct of war, when Canada is engaged in war, as the circumstances may require. It was also felt that it was part of his rights and responsibilities to delegate his powers as commander in chief to persons selected by him on the advice of his ministers; and that the commander of the Canadian army would have the right to take such measures as might be proper to deal with those who rendered themselves guilty of breaches of the usages of war. Persons had been apprehended who were charged with having committed war crimes against members of the Canadian forces, and the question arose as to how they would be dealt with.
War Crimes

A similar question, arose in the United Kingdom. There, by royal warrant under the sign manual of the sovereign, a war crimes court was set up to deal with offenders against members of the forces of the United Kingdom. This royal warrant seems to have been issued by His Majesty on the advice of one of his ministers. When the question arose here, the practice of royal warrants never having been adopted in this country, an order in council was passed to set up an authority to deal with those who had been apprehended and charged with offences contrary to the usages of war, committed against personnel 'belonging to the Canadian forces; and) the order in council determined, much along the lines of the regm lations approved by the royal warrant, the procedure to be followed.
In drafting the order in council reference was made to the War Measures Act. Shortly after it had been passed, a question was submitted to the Department of Justice for opinion, as to whether regulations made by this order in council were sufficient to enable penalties exceeding five years' imprisonment to be imposed. The officials of the Department of Justice went into the matter carefully and came to the conclusion that it was quite unnecessary and a surplusage to have had a reference to the War Measures Act in the order in council, and that even it would have been preferable, if it were mentioned at all, to mention it only as one of the statutory sources from which authority to make the regulations was derived1; and that without any reference to the War Measures Act the regulations could be properly made by the governor general on the advice, perhaps of even only one minister, but certainly on the advice of council.
There have been imposed sentences exceeding five years, and one of those sentences is being served now in a Canadian penitentiary by a German officer who had been apprehended, tried and convicted. There appeared, moreover, that there might be occasion to use these regulations beyond the time when the War Measures Act would operate. For that reason, and also to remove any possibility of doubt as to the validity, and continuing validity, of the sentences imposed, it was felt that it would be advisable to have the regulations which were made under the order in council reenacted by parliament. This bill is for the purpose of reenacting those regulations, although not necessarily as permanent legislation because, in spite of the gloomy picture international affairs sometimes present, it is not the policy of the government at this

time to envisage the necessity of maintaining legislation of this kind as permanent legislation.
It was, however, felt that it would be difficult to assign any specific date when it would be proper for the regulations to come to an end. So that the bill was drawn with the proviso that, if passed, it would continue in force until a day fixed by proclamation of the governor in council, and that from anS after that date it would be deemed to be repealed. The reason for using the language "be deemed to be repealed" is that that brings into play the Interpretation Act, which provides that whenever a statute is repealed, whatever has been done under it, if properly done, remains valid as a proper application of the act while it was in force.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider this bill one of unusual importance in that for the first time, so far as the parliament of Canada is concerned, it is actually giving to a court the power to take judicial notice of the laws and usages of war, which provisions are incorporated in section 10 (6).
While the minister says this is to be only a temporary measure, having regard to the inclusion of the principles and usages of war this measure is a really important step on the part of Canada in the evolution and development of international law, and the recognition by parliament of international law.
The circumstances under which this matter was first brought up were these: Someone drafted the war crimes regulations. Certainly no one in the Department of Justice did it. They made specific reference to the fact that the power being exercised by the governor in council was on the recommendation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, concurred in by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Defence, and under the authority of the War Measures Act.
In other words, while now the minister takes the view that these regulations were drafted as part and parcel of international law, or under the powers of His Majesty under royal warrant, the regulations provided that they were drafted entirely under the War Measures Act with the result-at least so I contended- that in view of the fact that penalties under the War Measures Act were restricted to five years or a fine of $2,000, no statute could grant to a subsidiary measure by way of order in council passed thereunder the power to impose a heavier penalty. Among others, Kurt Meyer, a prisoner in Dorchester penitentiary, might have made an application to the courts for

War Crimes
the purpose of determining that his imprisonment was illegal and, as a result, the doors of that penitentiary might have been opened, should the court find that an illegal sentence, beyond that provided for under the War Measures Act, had been imposed.
While the minister has said there was an opinion from the Department of Justice that such a possibility was not a probability. I would point out that in giving evidence on the matter before the committee on external affairs the deputy minister of justice said he had no doubt that a forceful argument could be made in support of the contention that I advanced to the contrary.
I think this is an important measure for two reasons: First, it will close the doors to the possibility of any war criminal, and Kurt Meyer in particular, being able to raise a defence now or hereafter that an illegal sentence has been imposed upon him; and, secondly, it represents I believe the first time a parliament in any country has taken upon itself the power to impose a penalty for the commission of an offence beyond the confines and territorial jurisdiction of that country. It is a new and unusual step, and one which I believe will be adopted generally in the en-forecemnt of international law in years to come by other countries. In my opinion one of the reasons for the developments that led to the second war was the fact that those who committed aggression crimes and offences against the laws and usages of war during the first world war remained unpunished. In some quarters objection is being taken to the fact that war criminals were being proceeded against, this objection being based upon the ground that international law is not written law and that, that law not having been formally established, procedure against war criminals is in the nature of revenge. In order to keep the record clear in that regard, I should like to point out that on August 21, 1942, President Roosevelt, on behalf of the government of the United States, advised the enemy countries at that time that any military commanders or other leaders who committed criminal offences would be subject to punishment. His statement was approved on September 8, 1942, by Mr. Churchill on behalf of the British government when he said.
I wish most particularly to identify the British government and the House of Commons with the solemn words which have been lately used by the President of the United States, namely, that those who are guilty of the nazi crimes will have to stand up before tribunals in every land where their atrocities have been committed in order that an indelible warning may be given to future ages and that successive generations of men may say, "So perish all who do the like again."
In this bill this house is taking a definite step forward in the development of international law which must be based upon international conscience, and founded upon the epitome of the idealism of all the peoples of the world possessed of an aroused conscience and appreciation of justice. The war trials do in the international field what has been accepted in the national field for many generations and assure that crimes committed by the great or their lieutenants in international wrongdoing shall be subject to punishment by the conscience and collective national will of states that have been offended against.
Usually I am opposed to retroactive legislation. However, I am sure that members on all sides of the house will accept this measure which ratifies what has been done and which assures that international wrongdoing shall not go unpunished. This measure maintains the rule of law in the international sphere. It assures that henceforth, as far as Canada is concerned, we inform the world that wrongdoing internationally will be subject to punishment when the nationals of this country are mistreated or are interfered with in their rights under international law.
The opening address of Mr. Justice Jackson of the United States in the case against the nazi war criminals may be of interest in this connection. He summarized the purpose of this bill in so far as the Canadian parliament is concerned when he used these words:
Civilization asks whether law is so laggard as to be utterly helpless to deal with crimes of this magnitude by criminals of this order of importance. It does not expect that you can make war impossible. It does expect that your juridical action will put the forces of international law, its precepts, its prohibitions and, most of all, its sanctions, on the side of peace, so that men and women of good will in all countries may have "leave to live by no man's leave, underneath the law."
In introducing this measure, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) has done much to assure that Canada will give not only lip adherence to the principles of international law but that this parliament is prepared by its passage to announce to the nations all over the world that Canada accepts the great principles of international law, founded on justice, on conscience and on the abiding principles that activate man in his national relationships in civil life.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee, read the third time and passed.
