speechtext:
As one who has taken some interest in the federal district commission ever since I was appointed a member of the committee which was set up to investigate it, I have one suggestion to make to the minister. I am not sure whether it is contained in the bill.
A short time ago I wrote to the Prime Minister suggesting a scheme which I believe would result in a greater interest being taken in the federal district of Ottawa and in the national capital, and that was that each provincial government be asked to take a part in the beautification of Ottawa and have on the board a representative from each province. My own province, for instance, could beautify a certain portion of parliament hill or of Mackenzie avenue, and other provinces could do likewise. Most members w'hen they first come here have a narrow viewpoint of Ottawa, being inclined to look upon it simply as Ottawa and not as the national capital. My membership on the committee certainly broadened my views, and since then I have looked at Ottawa from the national point of view. I have often asked myself how we could arouse a greater interest throughout the country in the development of Ottawa as the national capital, and I think one way would be to have the provinces improve and develop the grounds around the parliament buildings. My suggestion to the Prime Minister and to the Acting Prime Minister is that the scope of the bill be broadened so that each province may have a representative on the board. They would not need to meet more than about once a year.
I think everybody's attention was attracted this year by the grand display of tulips on the grounds in front of the parliament buildings. While it was stated that the tulip bulbs were a gift of good will by the people of Holland, the cold fact was that it was one of the best business displays that Holland ever made. I remember asking where the bulbs came from, and I was told that they were a gift from the people of Holland because they were so thankful for what Canada had done in the war. I investigated and found that
Eire had received as many bulbs from Holland as we had, and I asked myself what help Eire had given to Holland during the war. The answer was nil. I later discovered that some twenty good salesmen had left Holland and had come to the North American continent and that eight countries had been given great quantities of these beautiful bulbs. In British Columbia we have an excellent bulb which for many years has been finding a market in Ottawa, and now we find ourselves faced with competition with bulbs grown more cheaply in Holland, which have been displayed here under the guise of a contribution of thankfulness from the people of Holland. The cold fact was that it was a straight business deal by salesmen from Holland. I am not finding fault with the salesmen for that, because everyone must admit that the tulips were beautiful, but I had a sinking feeling when I thought of our bulb growers in British Columbia and what they would be up against from that competition. So I suggest to the Acting Prime Minister that each province be represented on the commission to stimulate a national interest in the capital city. I know there are men in British Columbia who are prepared now to take a spot on the parliament building grounds and' plant rose bushes and bulbs there, a display that, would be known as British Columbia's, and similarly with the other provinces. I think the suggestion has a great deal of merit and would arouse an interest in all the provinces in the beautification of Ottawa and in making it a real national capital. Unless we bring the provinces in, in some way, by giving them ^ direct representation on the federal commission and by encouraging oui* growers in the various provinces to see what they can do and take pride in the work I doubt very much whether the scheme will expand as fast as the Prime Minister has in mmd. Those are all the remarks I have to make at this stage. I would ask that consideration be given to the suggestions I have just outlined.

During the past number of years thousands and thousands of gift parcels have been sent by the people of Canada to the people of the old country. On all these gift parcels we are sending to Europe we have a rate which includes the charge we make ourselves, an amount to pay for the transit of those parcels, a certain amount which England asks when they pass through that country, and, in addition the charge made by the receiving nation. I had occasion this session to give the details of some of these rates. I am. speaking about parcels going direct to Great Britain, for people in Great Britain. I am not speaking of parcels that go to Great Britain first and then on to the continent. I understand that our rate on parcels going to Britain is twice the United States rate.

this is being discontinued. Surely these rural delivery men are under greater expense to-day than they were even during the war.

I shall answer that question immediately, because one might expect other questions along the same line. Only this afternoon a somewhat similar question was asked. Hon. members will realize, of course, that we have legal contracts with rural mail carriers and that we pay the bonus by virtue of order in council. These bonuses were supposed to be terminated on December 31, and we have asked to continue them until February 15. There is now before parliament a bill which would give the government an extension of sixty days instead of fifteen.
Some of the officials notified contractors that after the expiration of these contracts the bonuses could not be paid any longer because, unless we received authority from the House of Commons to do so, we would not have authority to continue the bonuses. Some of the officials gave this notification because they did not want to take any of the contractors by surprise. But after due consideration we are cancelling all these notices. We are sending a letter to every contractor who has received the notice telling him that we are hoping to continue the bonus until sixty days after the opening of the next session.
Then we shall have to readjust the contract either by asking for new tenders or by presenting a bill to parliament which would give the Postmaster General authority to renew these contracts at the rate set out therein, plus bonus. I do not want to plead the case before it comes up next session, but in order to prepare the hon. member I may say that every time we cancel a contract on account of the death of a contractor or to his sickness and inability to fulfil his contract, we ask for tenders. At this time the tenders are always higher than the original contract plus bonus.

I believe that in connection with rural mail delivery there is a basis of so much per mile, where a satisfactory service cannot be obtained otherwise. I understand that the department sometimes gives a mileage allowance. Is that basis higher to-day than it was three years ago; or is it on the same basis, plus the bonus being discussed?

The same basis, plus this bonus. Every time we ask for tenders it varies. I must admit that at certain times tenders are put in which are too low, but the law forces us to accept the tender of a man who has the facilities to fulfil his contract. The Post Office Act permits a postmaster to award a contract for $200 or less without asking for tenders. This provision

goes back to 1867. If we had had time this session I would have brought in amendments to the Post Office Act to increase this amount from $200 to $500, because I admit that to-day $500 is worth no more than $200 was in 1867.

In a case where a tender was too high and the department refused to accept it and then said that they had a mile rate which they thought was fair, the mile rate was the same as before the war. The department still insisted that it was quite fair and I am wondering why there was not some adjustment.

There is no fixed rate. We are obliged to take the lowest tender, but we are not obliged to take the highest. We have adjusted certain contracts on account of increased expenses caused by the war, but there is no fixed rate per mile. It would be impossible to fix a rate because so many factors enter into the contracts. In some places horses and sleighs must be used in the winter time and automobiles in the summer, while in other places aeroplanes are used and so on.

I should like to support the argument advanced by the hon. member for Kootenay West in connection with putting post offices in stores. When you ask the department to give this job to a returned soldier in a case where the storekeeper may be quite prosperous they write and tell you that you must get two people to give a sworn affidavit that the man is not operating the post office m the right way. That is not the point. The man is making money in his store and he is handling all the old age pension cheques and the children's allowance cheques. He knows where every cheque is going and when people come in for their cheques they are asked to pay their bills. This matter should be straightened out right now and every hon. member should support it. These people who keep stores should not be allowed to keep post offices, especially since the old age pensions and children's allowances have come into effect. I think every hon. member knows of cases, because there are thousands of them in Canada where the man running the store is keeping the post office. I think every hon. member in this committee should ask the Postmaster General to change the regulations whereby people running stores are allowed to keep post offices.
I hope the minister will not take that advice seriously.

If the hon. member for Vancouver wants to put up an argument against another member in his own party-

Supply-Post Office
Do not confuse me with Vancouver; it is New Westminster; please get it right.
I suppose he will vote against it because he always votes against his party.
I will say in a kindly way that I pity the hon. member and I ask the minister in all seriousness-
Somebody ought to pity you.
I do not care about that. I still say to the minister that I hope he does not take too seriously this suggestion. If it is followed many small places will not have post offices.

On page 11 of his report the Postmaster General reports a surplus of $11,442,000. The Toronto post offices contribute about thirty-one per cent of the gross revenue, since the statement on page 106 shows that the Toronto post offices contributed $12,290,055. During the war, the postmen on the routes had to serve twice as large a district as had been served during peace time. This placed a heavy strain upon the men, especially during the winter weather. A large number were laid off when the routes were doubled. This department has provided an excellent public service both in peace and in war. Along with the police and fire departments it is the other public utility giving most excellent service.
A large mail order post office building was built on Bay street, but the armed forces took it over during the war. I accompanied the predecessor of the present minister and the Postmaster General, along with the present Minister of Public Works, through terminal "A" post office building at Bay and Front streets, and we were both astonished at the conditions under which the staff had to work during rush times at Christmas and Easter. I understand that the department has now got part of this new mail order building back, and soon will have it all, so that a better building will give greatly needed space.
There used to be three deliveries each day in the business section and two in the residential section, and I should like to see this service restored. In some parts of the city they are getting only one residential delivery a day. Three years ago I complained about the punishment that was meted out to the one-tenth of one per cent of the men who got into trouble for stealing a few cents in letters. If a man took a few cents out of a letter the penalty imposed was three years. I brought this matter up for eight or nine years, and the act was finally amended making the punishment one year and giving the magis-63260-277
trate the option of reducing it to a lesser offence, with a penalty of one month, now the law. I think that is in the public interest and I am glad to see it is being carried out.
I should like to make a suggestion with regard to Toronto, and this may apply to other cities as well. We should have a system of drop letters at a one cent rate. There is no reason why that could not be done because there is a surplus of $11,442,000. I do not think the time is far distant when the rate will have to be reduced from three to two cents for letters going outside the city. Many complaints are being made about the cost of mailing parcels. The other day I sent the minister a letter which I had received from a prominent lady who is head of a patriotic organization. She sends about thirty or forty parcels a week to the old country and out of $4 or $5 she gets back only three or four cents change on maling only three of these. Probably tire rates are fixed at the other end by the British government, but the minister should look into this matter.
I hope the department will recover possession of the building on Bay street. I should like to say a word about branch post offices. There are a great many of them located in the twelve constituencies in Toronto. From 1869 to 1901 the department had deficits, but with few exceptions from then on it has always shown a surplus. There was a series of deficits in the depression years from 1927 to 1931, but the surpluses started again in 1932 when there was a surplus of $657,000. In 1933 this went up to $1,164,000, and in 1935 there was a surplus of $2,274,000. The surplus in 1938 was $3,249,000. During the war there were large surpluses. Last year the surplus was $12,585,000, and this year it is $11,442,000.
I believe the time has come for the Post Office Department to provide better working conditions for the rank and file of the staff. Perhaps that comes under the civil service commission. In any event, something should be done to improve the working conditions because they are deplorable. In the summer time the men wear heavy uniforms, almost as heavy as those of the mounted police. Suitable summer uniforms prevail in municipalities.
I believe that the Post Office Department, which has given such fine service both in peace and in war, should expand. It was about ready to expand when the war started. The post office in Great Britain and in France has made great improvements. Our post office should be extended, as in England, to other uses and functions, as a public utility and in that way the public would get more service. I hope that the minister will look

Supply-Post Office

into these matters, about which I wrote a memorandum to his predecessor, who said that he would certainly consider it. Certainly something should be done to provide better working conditions for the working classes who are engaged on this work. A large number of women and men also are now employed in sorting letters and doing other work inside, and their working conditions and space and health conditions are not at all what they should be. I was really surprised to see what those conditions were. You could not get away with them in a factory, but at terminal "A" in Toronto women are working by night and by day with insufficient lighting and lack of ordinary laws of public hygiene. I hope to see some modern improvements made in their working conditions.
In Toronto we have no main post office. We did once have a head post office on Toronto street, but we have no head post office in our city to-day. The department is leasing terminal "A", which is at the corner of Bay and Front street and is a part of the Union station. With a revenue of $13,000,000 from the Toronto post office, the city is certainly entitled to a modern post office building. Other public utilities have these new public buildings there; and it is not only a convenience but adds to the revenue as well.
I find some of the costly sub-post offices costing $20,000 to $30,000 or $40,000 with only about twenty per cent revenues therefrom. The department should be run on a commercial basis. I understand that the sub-post offices are granted and located on a party patronage basis, and not from a commercial aspect. Three hundred people applied for a new sub-post office on Carlaw avenue. They could not walk all the way from Gerrard street right up to Danforth, about a mile and a quarter, in bad weather, and they could not get a sub-post office on Carlaw avenue. I understand that the staff in sub-post offices is appointed on a party patronage basis. I have had a lot of complaints from returned men as to getting on terminal "A". I have had twenty or thirty letters from returned soldiers this year who were trying to get temporary or permanent employment at terminal "A". They could not apply there for work but had to go up to 465 Bay street, a mile farther away, to see somebody in the civil service commission. They would go in there and be kept waiting for half an hour or an hour and then be told to come back the next day, and they got no satisfaction. That should not be done to returned men, but I have seen it. There should be some more direct method of engaging these men. I do not believe

altogether in the civil service commission. It has made mistakes. I believe that the superintendent of the post office, Mr. Gibson, an able, efficient and popular director of Toronto, whose office brings in a revenue of $13,000,000 a year and who gets a small and insignificant salary for the work he dues, should have power as head of the branch to choose his own staff.
I venture to say that if he did, the returned men would get a better chance.

I cannot find any other item in the estimates on which to raise this important point, and so I take this opportunity of raising it on the administration item. I understand from outside sources that the Post Office Department is about to issue new postage stamps, and I am told that that there are seven new designs to be issued.
I made a statement in the house about the matter last week.

That is what I was coming to. Before the minister made his statement in the house and before the members had an opportunity of seeing these exhibits of beauty, a storm was brewing over the new designs, and I want to get the minister's point of view because it is essential that we should have both sides. One of the designs I * understand shows a ploughman with his furrow being turned on the wrong side of the plough. I have not seen the stamp myself. I think the members of the house should have been given a preview of these new designs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: A lefthanded plough.

If the minister ever
attempted to plough he would certainly take the wrong side of whatever he was doing. Perhaps he would be a left-handed ploughman.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Cincinnatus.

Another stamp depicts a logging scene. I am not prepared to express an expert opinion on this. No doubt my good friend the hon. member for 'Comox-Alberni and others will be able to do that. But the way we hear it is that this new stamp shows two loggers turning their backs upon a falling tree, which from the expert's point of view indicates that these two men are in great danger of their lives. Other criticisms as well have been made of the new stamps that are being issued. I should like the minister to indicate who was responsible for these stamps, who were the designers, and would he also indicate whether any changes are to be made? Perhaps in the end

Supply-Post Office
these stamps will provide additional money for the department. I certainly am not going to object to that. One paragraph that I read in the newspapers indicates that these new stamps will incidentally make money for the department. I quote one paragraph:
In all this, whatever the technical criticism, there is profit and enjoyment.
What paper is my hon. friend quoting from?

It is the paper that always supports my hon. friend, the Toronto Globe and Mail. It goes on:
Canadian stamps enjoy a world-wide reputation for their quality and a new issue almost always pays for itself three times over due to the demand of collectors, philatelists-
I may have the pronunciation wrong.
-are a peculiar brew who draw unbounded satisfaction from such things as inverted centres, over-impressions and double transfers. To them a left-handed plowman or a foolish woodsman is a thing of beauty and a joy forever.
I would ask the minister to enlighten the committee about these new objects of beauty which are shortly to adorn our letters.

As everyone knows, I am almost new in the office of Postmaster General. I never thought there were so many philatelists in the world, but long before this issue came out we received hundreds of letters asking us to reserve a certain number of postage stamps for the w'riters. We have here a fourteen cent stamp representing a hydro-electric plant on the St. Maurice river. It happens to be La Gabelle, one of the best known plants belonging to the Shawinigan Water and Power Company, and I have received telegrams from the company asking for a large number of these stamps to send as gifts, presumably to clients and friends of the company.
About the farmer in eastern Ontario, it is true that the gentleman who is ploughing the field there does it on the left. My attention has been drawn to that, but I am told that there are reversible ploughs; if somebody has to plough on the down hill he ploughs in such a way that the fallow falls downhill, not uphill.
Does that mean that the government is going downhill?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All the Tories are going downhill.

It is that way on this eight-cent stamp. I did ploughing myself when I was much younger, but I do not remember whether I was ploughing on the left or the right. However, according to the I Mr Brooks.]
63260-277J
philatelists, the picture of this plough turning on the left is moie valuable than if it were on the right side. There is no error; it is a very fine and well designed stamp.
Now about the fifty cent stamps; this issue 'shows lumberjacks working on fir and pine in British Columbia. I do not think there is any danger for these two men, because one is behind a tree-the tree is falling on the right and the man is behind it-and the other gentleman is cutting a tree which seems to be at least 150 feet on the right. The tree is falling to the rear, so that there is no danger at all. I do not think that stamp will have the value of the one which shows the plough working on the left.

I have two or three
questions to ask the minister. They are not interrelated in themselves, but they have relation to other questions which have been asked on this administration item, so I assume that I may present them. I was interested in hearing the minister say that the pay of the post office employees had been raised, and in that connection I want to mention the matter of overtime, the work performed on Sundays and on statutory holidays. I shall ask the minister this question, and invite him to reserve his answer while I go into another matter which has relation to it. My question is, do the post office employees now or can they hope shortly to draw overtime for work performed on Sundays or on statutory holidays-and I want to say this, and I want these words noted-in cash? One would wonder, if an employee is not paid in cash, what is the coinage in which he receives his remuneration. In looking into this matter I have unearthed something which surprises me tremendously.
I find that certain employees of the post office have agreements in that jime worked on statutory holidays-note this-"may at the present time be liquidated by time off'', and they urge that such liquidation be confined to the month in which the overtime is worked instead of spread over the month in which it is worked and the following month. That needs a little explaining to anyone like myself who is not familiar with that peculiar system.
I imagine it is pretty cold comfort to the letter carrier who wmrks overtime the night before Christmas to know that in the following February he shall get a Monday off for the service so rendered.
Mr. BER1 RAND (Laurier): He is paid in cash at Christmas time.

But only at Christmas time? However, perhaps I should let the minister answer my question: is there any
Supply-Post Office

provision now for overtime payment in cash for Sundays and statutory holidays? Would the minister at the same time comment upon this peculiar and, in my opinion, wrong system of paying a man by allowing time to be "liquidated"-a peculiar term which is apparently characteristic of the particular thing of which I am speaking? I should like the privilege of asking a further question when the minister has answered this one.
At all times, or at all events for some time, extra work done during the Christmas season has been paid for in cash.
Overtime?
Overtime.
Counting as time and a half?
At pro rata.
Not time and a half?

No. During the other periods of the year we were paying him in time off. I must tell the hon. gentleman that this question is being studied very carefully at present both by the department and by the treasury board. I cannot to-day give the decision at which we are going to arrive, but we are reviewing this matter after having reviewed the salaries.

The employees are desirous that this overtime or this "liquidation" of time should be paid in the month in which it is earned and not scattered over that month and the month which follows:
My other question has relation to the matter of parcel post. Someone brought up the subject to-night. I should like to refer to the sending of parcels by post to Germany. I know that ordinary letter mail to Germany was opened some time ago, and the United States opened a parcel post service some eight weeks ago. I applied to the Post Office Department to-day, and I will say that I got a civil and courteous answer from a gentleman in the minister's department, but while I got that information privately I think the matter ought to be brought to the attention of the house and the country. It is a matter affecting Canadian citizens and residents here who are anxious about the fate of their relatives in Germany. Germany, of course, is divided into three zones. I am thinking in particular of two of those zones, occupied respectively by British forces and by troops of the United States army. The letter I hold in my hand is written by a man who tells me that his mother died last year in January, 
simply from hunger. He has also sisters and a brother over there. It is only natural that he is desirous of sending small items of food and clothing, which he would not himself miss, in an attempt to save the lives of his remaining relatives. This afternoon I was given to understand by the official of the minister's department that the Post Office Department has done everything possible in that regard. Apparently they have applied to the United States authorities in the United States zone without success, and up until the present at least the result has been the same in the British zone. I presume that there is a way around this which is an irregular one. I presume that a man in this position could have food sent from the United States under the United States regulations, and it could be put into the zone now occupied by the United States army, but there would appear to be no way of getting food and clothing to save those people's lives in the British zone. It is a matter which concerns many people of German origin in this country, and I would urge the minister to keep on with the good work of trying to break down these walls at the earliest possible moment and thereby save lives.

I wish to say a few words about this. Ever since the war terminated we have had a lot of requests to send parcels to the former enemy countries of Germany and Italy, but we did all we could to accommodate our own people. There was no service in these countries. Even France, which was liberated some time before the end of the war, was in a similar position. We could not send parcels there because the French authorities had no way of delivering them. We started up by sending a small parcel of four pounds; then the weight was increased to seven pounds, then to eleven pounds and now it is twenty-two pounds. These services are being reorganized as quickly as possible in these countries, and as soon as we get the green light we shall be glad to notify the public of Canada that they may send parcels to these countries.

I may say to the minister , that I have no complaint about the design of the new postage stamp for New Brunswick because there is no such thing. The same applies to Nova Scotia. I might tell the minister, if he has not already heard it, that both these provinces feel that they have been neglected. When the minister was considering designs he might very well have considered New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, especially when we realize what these provinces did during the war. I might refer particularly to the ports of Saint John and Halifax. No port in

Supply-Post Office
Canada did as much for the war effort as did the port of Halifax, and to a lesser degree the port of Saint John.
It is a better port.

It does not make any difference which is better; they are both good, and they are both good enough to be considered when stamps are being designed. I know the minister will tell us that'he has given us a stamp for the maritime provinces. I believe that stamp represents the new ferry boat between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Is that not correct?
That is absolutely correct, and it is a beautiful one.

The hon. member for Queens will probably tell the minister that they would rather see this ferry on the Northumberland strait than on a postage stamp. They have been waiting a long time for that ferry and I believe it will be some time yet before it is on that route. Therefore, if there is any criticism-
According to the stamp she seems to be going fine.

She is going at Sorel; but, if I understand correctly, it is not on the route between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
My main object in rising was to ask the minister a question in reference to village post offices. We have made application for a number of post offices in my own province. I refer particularly to the village of Rothesay in the county of Kings, New Brunswick. This is a village of nearly two thousand people, one of the few incorporated villages in the maritime provinces. They have post office accommodation which would disgrace a rural community of a hundred or a hundred and fifty people. There is a small room; it is not much larger than, I was going to say, a telephone booth. When the people go for their mail no matter what the weather is like, if there are more than three or four some have to stand outside. In this village there are two large schools, the Rothesay collegiate school for boys and the Netherwood school for girls, and also a large consolidated school. I know of no other community anywhere that I have been in in Canada which has as poor postal accommodation as has the village of Rothesay. I wrote not only to the Post Office Department but to the public works department some time ago, and the excuse that was given was that they were not building any post offices during the war. That was a reasonable excuse; but during the war our Post Office Department must
have made considerable money, and I know no reason why something should not be done along this line. If a new post office is not constructed-and I contend that they are * deserving of a new post office-at least some suitable accommodation should be provided. The revenue from this village is over $8,000 a year, and I am satisfied that it cannot be costing more than half of that to carry on the postal services.
I might also say to the minister that a short time ago I sent him a petition from the village of Rothesay asking for a new post office, and as yet I have not had the courtesy of a reply from the minister's department. It may be that he has not had time, but the ' petition was sent.
When was the letter sent?
It was sent ten days ago, and that should be sufficient time. If the minister has not had time to reply that is perfectly all right.
We may have to make an investigation; we generally make an investigation.

As I say, I wrote the department before. The offices in Ottawa should have all the information which is required; it should not take long to make an investigation.
I should also like to take up the matter of rural routes. Possibly what applies to my constituency applies to a great many. Very little has been done during the war to extend rural routes throughout the country. A good many applications have been made for an extension, but the reply we have received is that there has been a war on and they could not extend these rural routes. I hope that the minister will take under consideration the many applications which he must have for the extension of rural routes for the better postal accommodation of the people throughout the country. I do not think there is anything further other than these two items. I hope that the minister will give them his attention and look into the matter of the Rothesay post office.

I do not wish to delay the committee in the passing of these estimates, but I feel that I should give an answer to the hon. gentleman with reference to the stamps. We have nine new stamps. Of course we cannot at all times have a stamp-

I would point out that there are only nine provinces in Canada.
Supply-Post Office

Yes. If the hon. gentleman wishes to hear my answer I shall be glad to give it to him. When we print stamps we cannot at all times print nine, one for each province. We have to take care of the large province of Ontario in which is situated Toronto, which produces over $13,000,000 of revenue. It is true that in this issue there is no stamp having particular reference to Nova Scotia. There is one, as the hon. member said, depicting a ferryboat proceeding from Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick or vice versa. It is a beautiful stamp. We take our motif from the different districts, and I must say that as long as I am Postmaster General I shall never forget either Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. I like those two provinces very much; I know their importance, and I am sure that hon. members representing those provinces do not let anyone forget them. We have paid our respects to Nova Scotia in years gone by. In 1938, /or example, we had a stamp showing Halifax 'harbour. In 1929 we had beautiful stamps of -the Bluenose, and in 1930 we had a stamp showing Grand Pre. In 1934 we had a New "Brunswick stamp showing a ship, and we had *one of Prince Edward Island in 1935. I am *sure the objection raised is not very serious, '.but we like io show we are not forgetting New Brunswick or Nova Scotia.
With regard to post offices in villages, as the hon. member knows they are revenue post offices, meaning that the postmaster receives a percentage of the revenue. In places where the revenue may be only $50 or $60 a year we pay the postmaster a minimum of $110, losing money thereby. I know the postmasters have to furnish decent places to keep the post offices, and the department does not look after those places, though we pay a certain amount by way of subsidy. In the case of Rothesay, if the hon. member has had no reply it is probably because there have been complaints and we have asked the district director to make a report; because if it is not large enough, or .if it is not convenient having regard to the size of the village, we shall have to ask the postmaster to find another place.
With regard to the post office building, the hon. member answered the point when he argued his case. At this time, when material is so scarce, we cannot expect to build many post offices. I must admit that we are far behind in the construction of these buildings because of the war years. We have received three or four hundred requests for new post office buildings; the population of many towns has increased, and a certain number- I will not say too many, because it might
cost us a great deal of money next year-of buildings will have to be erected at points where the revenue is $10,000 or more. The revenue at Rothesay is $7,270. Before the war, and especially before the first world war, if a member of parliament attended the sessions regularly, and I suppose voted correctly, sometimes he could get the public works department to build a post office, but I must say that in my department we are trying to follow one of the rules that have been suggested quite often by hon. gentlemen opposite, a rule called economy. The demand is so great that we have had to make some rules, and we shall not 'be able to build post offices where the postal revenue is not at least $10,000.
May I ask when that rule was put into effect, because I know post offices that have been built where the revenue is much less than $10,000.

As I said, before the war there was no fixed and strict rule as there is to-day. I do not say we shall not depart from that rule. We would depart from it if it were necessary in order to give work to more men in the country, and so on; but at the present time, with the shortage of materials, we would1 be severely criticized if we started to put up three or four hundred post office buildings all over Canada. A little patience will surely cure many of these things.
As to the rural routes, we are providing as many as possible, but again we have to consider the cost. We have had to cut down certain rural routes in some parts of the country where perhaps only two or three families were being served in a distance of three or four miles. It was very difficult to cut them down, and we have heard about it ever since, but we must be careful with the people's money. Any time we find a situation where there are four farmers or four postal addresses, as we call it, per mile, we extend the route whenever possible. If the roads are impassable of course we will not do it, but we do extend routes where conditions permit. I must say that in years gone by postmasters general were very kind to the people of New Brunswick, because they have a good share of the rural routes.

I should like to ask a question with regard to the matter which was discussed when these estimates came up first; that is, the postal rates on parcels to the old country. In his breakdown the minister gave us the figure of $2.25 for an 11-pound parcel, of which forty cents went to our post office, sixty cents to Great Britain and $1.25 in shipping charges. Those shipping charges seem

Supply-Post Office
to me quite excessive, because that would be at the rate of approximately $500 a ton, and at that rate it would cost $12 to ship a bushel of wheat from Saint John to Liverpool. I wonder how long that rate has been in effect. Is it a rate that was put on during the war, and what companies are enjoying this rate? It seems to me excessive, and I should like an explanation.
While I am on my feet, I should like to ask another question. The minister stated that to establish a rural route would require four farmers to the mile. I do not believe that rule applies in western Canada. We would not have any rural routes out there if it required four subscribers to the mile. I am just wondering what the rule is there and what extensions have been made in western Canada in the past year.

When I was speaking of four farmers per mile I was answering the hon. member for Royal, in regard to the east. Of course I admit that in the west we have to be more generous in this, as in some other things.
The rate for parcels is according to weight and also according to the number of cubic feet. We pay seventy-five cents per cubic foot. As the hon. gentleman knows, these parcels sometimes contain clothing and articles that are quite heavy, and I understand that it takes one and a half or two cubic feet for each parcel.
How long have these rates been in effect? Have they been in operation for a number of years?
Since the beginning of the war.
There has been no reduction in the rate since the end of the war?

There will be, I am sure. We are trying to get better rates, and as soon as the new lines begin to operate we may do so. To-day, as the hon. gentleman knows, all the ships are crowded, and I do not expect any reduction before another five or six months.

I thought I should rise when I heard some slight criticism regarding the new stamps. However, it was friendly criticism. I wish to say that we appreciate very much the beautiful design on the stamp given to my province, a stamp which happened to be the most expensive one. But, joining with the hon. member for Royal, how much more would we appreciate it if the Postmaster General were to jog the memory
of his colleague, the Minister of Transport, and ask him when he is going to give us a steamer between Tormentine and Borden?
Order.

I should like to offer a suggestion regarding the bonuses the rural carriers are being paid. These bonuses were most acceptable to them and, as other hon. members have said, the cost of living is still going up. It would not be in their interests to have the cut at the present time. The Postmaster General has told us that possibly sixty daj-s after the next session some legislation in this connection will be introduced. I would suggest, however, that the bonus be continued until the expiration of the contracts. When tenders are called there will be an opportunity for re-tendering and for getting probably more than the five per cent bonus. Or perhaps the Postmaster General has something better in mind for the rural carriers.

I have before me a letter from the Peterborough district council of the civil service federation of Canada. On more than one occasion they have suggested that the Postmaster General see to it that the regulations respecting the size of envelopes be enforced, and that the standard size of envelopes be used. They object to the use of small envelopes and cards such as are used at Christmas and other holiday seasons. The sorters and the letter carriers have great difficulty in looking after these outsize letters and post cards. I would ask the Postmaster General to check on this.
On many occasions I have had letters from people in my constituency respecting the stamping of picture post cards by the post office. They tell me that in most cases they receive picture post cards on which the Post Office Department has placed its stamp, thereby rendering the pictures useless. Only the other day I received a beautiful post card from Italy-I believe it was handpainted -and the only postmark on the picture side of the card was a Canadian postmark. The other marks had been placed on the address side. I suggest that a regulation should be put through to stop the defacing of picture post cards.
I believe the question of sub-post offices is of interest to every city of any size where sub-post offices are used. If I mail a letter in the general post office in Peterborough to any one of the sub-post offices in that city I must place a four-cent stamp on it. For instance, if this chamber were the city of
Supply-Post Office

Peterborough and if my seat were the general post office and I were to post a letter from my seat, sending it to the minister who, we will say, is in a sub-post office, I would have to place a four-cent stamp on it. But if I were to post a letter addressed to the house [DOT]next door to the sub-post office I would have to use only a three-cent stamp. If a party has to call for it at the sub-post office the rate is four cents. This is confusing, because letters are sent out not only by myself but by other people, addressed to sub-post offices. We find that those receiving the letters or calling for them have to pay the additional postage.
Then, according to the district director, an overweight letter sent to a sub-post office must pay two cents for each additional ounce. I believe that all letters posted to any point in a city, whether or not they be addressed to a sub-post office, should pay the same rate of three cents.
I came across an article in the Popular Science magazine of March, 1946, which states that a new federal law in the United States has authorized the postmaster general there to offer anything up to $1,000 to any postal employee in return for a top-grade invention. Such, suggestion must either promote economy or increase efficiency so that it m-ay be adopted by the post office department. As at present understood, there will be no time limit placed on the contest, but the total amount of the reward under the act must not exceed $25,000 in any one year. Further regulations are to be worked out under the postmaster general in that country. I believe that our postal system in Canada works well, as does that in the United States. However, I believe our Postmaster General might take that suggestion into consideration, and see what can be done with it.
What was the total revenue for the post office department last year?
There was a gross revenue of $83 million.

During the war, as a war measure postage was increased from three cents to four cents. Does all that four cents go to the 'Post Office Department?
Perhaps one of the reasons the revenue for the department was up lies in the fact that service pins sent out by the Department of National Defence had postage paid on them, as well as an additional ten cents for registration. Do other departments in the government put postage stamps on their mail?

I appreciate the hon. member's suggestion concerning rewards. Of course in the United States where

the revenue is so tremendous they can offer amounts that we could not afford to offer here.
You could make the amount smaller.

Last year we held a conference of district directors and we intend to repeat this conference every year. This was the first time that it was held, and a large number of suggestions were made which we will consider during the year and try to implement. With regard to the cost of a drop letter, which is a letter dropped in a region where there is a post office, I would say that that is three cents. The cost of a forward letter, which has to go to another post office, is four cents.
This was right in the city, from one post office to another.

I do not know the exact situation in Peterborough, but I shall ask the superintendent to make a report. I would be surprised if what the hon. member calls a sub-post office is really a subpost office as we understand it in the department. It must be another post office serving another region.
I am referring to sub-office No. 1, which is situated right in Peterborough.

I will make
inquiries.
Will the minister answer the other question about the envelopes?

We are trying to settle that question, because the suggestion was made to us at the conference. It would be difficult to have a fixed and drastic rule, but we are trying to work it out by making arrangements with the manufacturers of envelopes.

I hesitate to enter into a profound discussion like the one we have had this evening, but I shall do my best. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. members for Broadview and Davenport of the city of Toronto who referred to the mail service there. I should like to point out that, apart from the north pole, I think my riding has probably the slowest service of any riding in Canada. On the west coast of Vancouver island it is desperate. The minimum time for an ordinary first-class letter is six days, while the maximum will run as high as sixteen days. Is there any possibility of the minister allowing members of parliament the privilege of franking their letters for air mail when it is going a thousand

Supply-Post Office
miles or more from Ottawa? The electors of Comox-Alberni and other British Columbia ridings, and those in other constituencies far away, are entitled to a more rapid service. I would appreciate it if the minister would give this matter consideration.

The matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is related to the question raised by the hon. member for Wentworth who referred to the cancellation of the war bonus paid to rural mail carriers. I should like to refer to what are known as mail couriers; that is, the persons who carry the mail from the post office to the train and from the train to the post office. Their contract does not amount to very much, but I understand that recently they received notice that the war bonus was to be cancelled and that the contract would be renewed only on the basis of the figure that prevailed before the war. Most of these mail couriers are old veterans and the amounts they receive are not large. Many of them have no other income, and I think the minister should continue the bonus at least for the time being. I should like to ask whether these mail couriers are in the same position as the rural mail carriers?
Yes.

I should like to inquire about the policy of the post office with respect to the use of the mails by charitable and other organizations in connection with puzzle contests. Many communities are endeavouring to raise funds for memorial centres by means of puzzle contests. The Post Office Department has ruled, I believe as of February 15, that the mails cannot be used for this purpose. The result is that in some cases those conducting the contest are unable to reply to entrants and they are now being branded as dishonest. I understand that this action is being taken in order to safeguard the public against institutions that might be working dishonestly. Apparently the Post Office Department have decided that, whether or not a contest is actually illegal, if an attempt is made to mislead the public they rule that it is matter which cannot use the mails.
I suggest that this decision ought to be left to the courts. If it is government policy that people are to be protected from illegal contests, then I submit that they should go to the courts to decide whether or not a contest is illegal instead of trying to do through the post office regulations what apparently they feel they cannot do under other legislation. As I say, many of these institutions have lost potential money and certainly their reputation has been injured. Would the minister consider revising that rule?
The hon. member is referring to the Kamloops recreation centre, or something like that?
That occasioned my question, but I was referring to the matter in a general way.

In the Post Office Act there is a section which prohibits the use of the mails for lotteries. I must admit that probably we are unable to stop all lotteries immediately they start; sometimes it takes a few weeks and sometimes we do not know that the mails are being used for a lottery. In the last year or so these lotteries have increased tremendously and many complaints have been received from all parts of Canada. I was obliged to make a public announcement in the newspapers about a week or two ago notifying the public that we could not allow the use of the mails for lotteries. We stopped all mail and returned it to the point of mailing. We have been asked by some of these people to give them the letters rather than return them to the senders, but we could not do that because the section is mandatory and we have to obey the law. The gentleman in charge of the Kamloops recreation centre saw me and the officials of the department, and when he left he told us he was satisfied that he could not keep on with what he had been doing.

Admittedly there is power under the Post Office Act in so far as lotteries are concerned. I discussed the matter with the deputy minister, and I am quite satisfied that there is power to rule against an organization running a lottery. My point is that if it is not a lottery, if it is not a game of chance, there is no such power.
If it is a game of chance it is a lottery.

If the Post Office Department receives a complaint that there is a lottery, that there is something illegal about the contest, then I suggest that, instead of using that arbitrary power in cases of doubt, it should advise the complainant to take the matter to the courts. If it is an illegal contest or gambling game there are statutes prohibiting that sort of thing and the case can be settled in the courts. It seems to me that the Post Office Department is in danger of using one of these regulations for a purpose never intended; that is, to stop games of skill or chance. I am glad' to say that the deputy postmaster general advised me that there was nothing dishonest about this puzzle contest, and I presume he is still of the same opinion. But I am not basing my position
Supply-Post Office

on an individual case, because I do not think that individual cases should! be made the subject of appeals across the floor of the house. But a principle is involved, and inasmuch as many of these contests may be conducted perfectly honestly and without breaking any of the laws of the country I am suggesting to the Postmaster General that he advise his complainants that if they think there is anything illegal about it there are courts provided for the purpose and he should not enforce a regulation which deprives many communities of funds for useful purposes.

I do not think we did anything that was arbitrary. I must tell the hon. gentleman that I was crown prosecutor in Montreal for seventeen years and I have seen a lot of these things. We will never stop the mails when they are carrying something which is not contrary to the Post Office Act. Of course I do not agree with the hon. member in his opinion about this particular case. There is no doubt at all in my mind thatdt was a lottery.

I think the minister is to be commended for not allowing the mails of Canada to be used1 for sweepstakes or lotteries. I know that the opposition will support him in this because they do not believe in spending a dollar to take a chance on winning several thousand. The minister should feel that the House of Commons is behind him in this, and that a big section of this country will not tolerate lotteries or anything of that sort

For some considerable time past I have had a certain amount of correspondence from the federated association of letter carriers in Calgary. I think the Postmaster General will be relieved to know that I am not going to ask for a new post office or anything like that. During the recess I met a considerable number of these men at their request and found them a most conscientious and earnest group of men who seem to be troubled over certain matters which they were anxious to have brought to the attention of the Postmaster General and parliament. Accordingly I have a few questions to direct to the Postmaster General. First is the matter of retirement of men who have already expressed a wish to retire, provided that superannuation is available for them. This whole subject became a live one amongst them because of a notice which was posted up in the Calgary post office on February 22, 1945, which read:
With a view to creating positions in the postal service for returned soldiers the department is desirous of ascertaining the number of

vacancies which will be created in the near future. While permanent employees are at present required to furnish schedule "J" before they can be retired on superannuation, there is a possibility that some changes may shortly be made in the regulations.
Will all employees who would be interested under these conditions please submit a written request to me at the earliest possible moment?
I would ask the Postmaster General whether any action has been taken with regard to that matter. Apparently up to April of this year nothing further had been done. The notice had been posted up and the men's minds were cohsiderably perturbed. Some put in a request for retirement and others were wondering whether to do so or not. May I have an answer from the minister stating just what the position is now?

That was done before my time but I suppose I am responsible. It was exploratory'. We wanted to know if it was worth while passing any regulation about it. Very' few answered, according to my information, and it did not materialize in any rule or regulation of any kind.
I take it that nothing further has been done about the matter. Have those who put in their application been told whether they would be retired on superannuation, or have they not?
I cannot say at the moment. I will look into the matter.

The next question is as to hours of duty. I do not know anything about the hours of duty in the post office; but, so far as I can make out, the position of these men was this. The tour of duty in the postal service is at present on the basis of eight hours a day, while the rest of the civil service enjoys a six and one-half hour day. Their contention is that, as part of the civil service, their tour of duty should be on the same basis, namely, six and one-half hours a day. I do not know whether that is a practical request or whether it could be readily put into execution, but it does seem a bit out of line that these men comprise the only large group in the civil service which works an eight-hour day as compared with six and a half hours for the rest of the service.
They get higher pay, which is not to be forgotten, than do those who are working a fewer number of hours. They also get a larger increase than the others. Most of them got the maximum increase.
What is the rate of pay of these letter carriers? I have never understood that it was particularly good.
They start at SI,320 and go up to SI,800, plus the cost of living bonus.

Another matter on their minds is the present system of ninty per cent permanent and ten per cent temporary appointments. Apparently the system used to be that 100 per cent of the appointments would be permanent. I understand that that was done away with; I do not know how long ago. Now ninety per cent are permanents and ten per cent temporaries, and the temporaries do not receive as much pay and are not eligible for superannuation benefits. Is that rule still in effect, and, if so, how long is it to be kept in effect? Or is it a permanent regulation?

During the
war we were not allowed to make permanent appointments. We had to take on temporaries because we wanted to replace these men by returned soldiers. Some employees in certain categories were made permanent. But we keep at least ten per cent as a cushion for an increase of work. In most of the post offices the work fluctuates according to the period of the year, and it has always been the practice to keep a cushion to meet changes in the amount of work.
I hardly think that is a satisfactory explanation. I know of at least one case of a man at Calgary who has been on the temporary staff for twelve or fifteen years.
He may not have passed the examinations. To be permanent one has to pass the required examinations, and some of these men have not done so.

There is no question of his not having passed the examination. He has been on the job, but he has not been able to enjoy the benefits of permanency in spite of the fact that he has been working there for twelve to fifteen years. It seems to me that a system like that is a poor one, and calculated to break down the morale of the employee.
If the hon. gentleman will give me the name of this person I will look into the case and give him a direct answer.

It is a system which should be done away with. If a man is doing a particular job he should be put in that job and enjoy the pay and status of that job, and if he is not able to do it, get rid of him and engage somebody else. A man should not be
Supply-Post Office
kept hanging around in a position where more or less he does not know what the score is or what is going to happen to him.
The only other point I wish to mention is connected with statutory holidays, which apparently, so far as post office employees are concerned, were cancelled shortly after the commencement of the war. I should like to know whether those statutory holidays have been restored to these men, and, if not, when they will be.
They have been.
I want, if I can, to get an answer to this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I want to say a word about this debate. I think it is time we knew where we stand. I heard last week in this house nothing but the cry, with which I have a lot of sympathy, for "economy, economy, economy". Now we have a different cry, for additional expenditures in regard to all the departments of government. We cannot reconcile these two things; and I think, if we are to finish this session in a reasonable time, we should get on with this work in a reasonable manner and conclude these debates.
Mr. Chairman, I take objection to the remarks of the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no personal reflection.	.

I was not in any instance calling for greater expenditure; I was presenting the complaints of a certain number of my constituents, which I consider it is my duty to do, in this house. I take strong exception to the minister making that an excuse for saying that I, or any other members of this party, have been talking economy in the past and are now talking with exactly the opposite effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that there was no personal reflection.
I am sorry that I did not understand at once the last question of the hon. member. The holidays have now been restored.
Thank you.

I should like to bring up a couple of questions at this time. They are not related, but in order to facilitate business I will put them together. This does not call for expenditure, either.
I am in much the same spot as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, in that I come from an area of the west coast which has
Supply-Post Office

poor facilities for the delivery of mail, namely Queen Charlotte island. There is a boat that goes in every ten days. The people cannot mail on the same boat the answers to the letters they receive, so that there is a lapse of twenty days between a letter being sent and answered. There is an aeroplane service in there now, but it is not on a scheduled basis. As I understand the rule regarding transport of mail, it must be done by aeroplanes on schedule, not just on charter work. But to all intents and purposes these aeroplanes are on a regular schedule, although not listed as such. The people at, say Massett, would like to have air mail now that aeroplanes are calling regularly there. I have no doubt that it would help the company which has inaugurated that service. But when one inquires of the department they say that there are certain regulations which, the air transport authorities demand, that the service be in operation six months, and so on and so forth. We are under an economy of private enterprise where we have "get and go". I should like to see that maxim applied to the Post Office Department. Cannot they brush away the red tape in a special case in an isolated area? Granted that you must have a lot of red tape in highly congested areas where there are transcontinental lines and other facilities, here you have an isolated area which should not be subject to the general rule. I hope the department will look into the matter and cut the red tape, so that these planes can pack mail up to these people at Queen Charlotte, Massett and Port Clements.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister the problem of the people of Atlin. I am not going to ask him to spend any money, but this is a case of a few nails. They have a building there, but it is not adequate for the purpose. There is very little standing space in the post office, and they have to stand outside in the winter time while their mail is being sorted, but there would be plenty of space in the post office if the wickets were moved back. There is an old Indian office which is not in use that could be made into a general waiting room for these people, so that they could stay inside and be comfortable in the winter weather. Outside; the sidewalk slants into the post office, and there is a pool of water there; they have to be regular puddle jumpers to get in, and if there was just a shanty roof put over it, it would save a good deal of wet feet and so on which is very hard on elderly people. I hope the minister will give consideration to these two matters.

I appreciate the remarks of the Minister of Veterans Affairs in wanting to get on with the business of the house, but I understand it is the business of the house to debate these matters, even though after we have spoken we do not convince anybody; and that is not personal either. The minister has a habit of hitting a person in the solar plexus and then saying, "Nothing personal; nothing personal about that!"
I want to ask one question, and then you can pass all the post office estimates that you want. The minister was talking some little while ago about rates for overseas parcels. I am not so much concerned about the rates, but the weight of these parcels is limited to eleven pounds each, and of those eleven pounds there is a limit of seven pounds of food. I could never see why that should be. The people in England particularly are in need of food; yet when we wrap up a parcel, in order to get full advantage of the eleven pounds we have to stuff it with a lot of other things because we are not allowed to send eleven pounds of food. Could the minister not change that regulation a little? Then, I believe they are allowed only one parcel a month. There are ways of getting around this, by sending one parcel to your sister and another to your brother and another to your grandmother; but why is each person allowed only one parcel a month?
I have one more question. Has the minister ever given any consideration to the subject of anonymous letters passing through the mails? I do not know what he can do about them; but may I go so far as to suggest that if it were made a criminal offence, perhaps people would not take the chance in sending anonymous letters through the mails. I always assume that when letters are sent anonymously there is mischief somewhere, and if something could be done to curb that practice it would be a good thing. But I am particularly interested in the matter of food for people in England.

I explained a few minutes ago that the limitation of food to seven pounds per parcel and the limitation of one parcel per month are restrictions imposed by the receiving nation. None of these restrictions is imposed by us, and since we are sending the parcels we have to abide by the rules which are imposed on us; otherwise they would not be delivered.
Then the receiving nations should change their rules.

I believe as the hon. gentleman does, but the receiving nations do not.

Supply-Post Office

Under the heading "departmental administration", there are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister. I do so with some fear and trembling because of the humour expressed a few moments ago by the leader of the house. I wish to compliment the Postmaster General on the reply which he gave earlier to the hon. member for Kootenay West, when he said that so far as he was concerned veterans would have pre-' ference in post office matters. I compliment him because, since I came into the house a few years ago, I remember an instance in my county when two fine veterans of the first war applied for a post office position, and a young man who had never seen service got the office. It was something of which I was ashamed to speak.
The matter to which I wish to refer specifically has to do with thickly populated suburban areas outside a city which has a letter carrier service. The area is adjacent to the city but not within its municipal boundaries. The people in that area have to go a long way to the post office. In the one instance I have in mind one rural route goes through the area. Since the population is growing, there is a demand for some service. What is the governing factor in that regard?
Another matter to which I wish to refer is the extension of rural routes. Frequently we find a good class of farmer or two living up a road which would be called a dead-end, which means that if the courier went up he would have to retrace his steps. These people are retepayers and are just as much entitled to postal service as the other people. It is quite a hardship for them to come out and get their mail. Perhaps they may get a letter which requires a reply. They have to go back before the man returns the next day; they cannot stand on the corner waiting. These are matters of policy on which I should like to have the minister's opinion.

I wish to comment a little on the work of the post office. I listened with interest to the discussion on the postage stamps. I was going to commend the minister for doing uphill work with a downhill plough.
I also wish to comment on the extension of rural routes. In my riding I have an application for the extension of a route, but -most of the people live within a half mile of an already established route, and while there were seventeen within the half mile the route could not be extended which seems too bad.
Then there is the question of drop letters. In London, for instance, a drop letter is delivered for three cents. Many people in
London mail a letter thinking that, because it is in London, it will be delivered for three cents; but when the farmer out on the rural route gets it he has to pay two cents more for it. I think that might well be changed.
I also appreciate what will be done with regard to the wartime bonus for rural mail carriers.

May I revert for a moment to the new issue of stamps? How were the designs selected? Who made the designs? Were a number of designs submitted and considered and then a choice made? I ask these questions because I am one of those people who are critical of the designs which appear on our Canadian stamps. If you compare the designs of the Canadian stamps of the past number of years with the designs of some of the stamps of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick prior to confederation, or some of the other provinces prior to confederation, or if you compare the designs of our present-day stamps with some of the designs of the Canadian stamps after confederation you will find that really they are not comparable. They do not compare in design, in colour or in texture. It seems to me that more consideration might be given to the designs of our Canadian stamps in order to make them more artistic and more effective.
I do not know whether it is a good plan to have designs depicting different parts of Canada. Some complaint has been made about that this evening. Some complaint has been made that there was no design for Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. I am not going to harp on that this evening. It seems to me that perhaps we might show more imagination or more vision if we are to depict these regional designs. We might perhaps very well picture the future developments of our provinces. So far as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are concerned, the minister might put on one of these stamps a design showing the new Chi-bucto canal which I presume is to be built before very long, or the power development on the Petitcodiac river or the new-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Canso ferry.
Canso bridge.

Or the new airport at Clover Valley, near Saint John, which I understand is to be constructed before very long. Another good design would be one depicting the free port which will be established at the port of Saint John in the near future.

I must admit that the hon. member for St. John-Albert has a good imagination, but if we were making
Supply-Post Office

these designs we might be told by the Canadian people that we were discounting the future too much.
With regard to the designs, they were made by our officials. I must tell the hon. gentleman that among the philatelists our stamps are considered the best in the world.
I do not agree with them.

Well, I shall give the hon. gentleman an example. Recently the collection of the late President Roosevelt was put up for sale by a broker in New York and the stamp which brought the largest amount of money was a Canadian stamp which was issued during the war. It brought $1,167 out of a collection which sold for over $227,000. I give that to the hon. gentlemen as an example, and if I hold my present position for very long I shall probabl'y be able to give him other examples.

It is interesting to note that as a rule the thing which makes a stamp valuable is that there is something wrong with it. I am not sure that it is a good thing to say that the Canadian stamps are the most valuable in the world. Does the Postmaster General know what was wrong with this particular stamp?

Reverting from new stamps to old ones, may I ask the minister what was the total revenue of the philatelic division during the last fiscal year? W hat was the cost of operating it? If the minister has these figures I should like to have them. There are several other questions I should like to ask later.
I shall have those figures in a moment.

Very well. Then, may I ask the minister a more important question. Of the total number of employees of the Post Office Department, what percentage is temporary? I ask this question because I should like some information in regard to this policy of the Post Office Department, and I believe some other government departments, of keeping ten per cent of the employees on a temporary basis instead of giving them permanent places. I wish to follow that question with one as to the number of permanent appointments made in the Post Office Department during the last fiscal year. While his deputies are obtaining that information, I wonder if the minister could tell the committee just how severe the fluctuations are in the revenues of the Post Office Department. Do they fluctuate pretty well with the national income of the country, or is there a relatively 
steady flow of revenue to his department? If the fluctuation is not severe I should think the ordinary mortality and retirement rate would allow for men who have served for three or, at the most, five years having their positions made permanent.

The revenue does fluctuate, at least to a certain extent. In the Post Office Department we have a barometer of business in Canada which is recognized as pretty good and sound. It is the total of the money orders and postal notes sold each year. I may tell the hon. gentleman that this year we have the highest amount in our history. These postal notes and money orders are sent by people who do not ordinarily send cheques; that is, the small people, and this year that total is S498,000,000. In the years of the depression it fluctuated a great deal, I understand. The money we received for mail transit last year increased quite considerably also, owing to the fact that there is more international correspondence. So that there are a number of factors which make the revenue fluctuate quite a bit.

In regard to the question of sending parcels overseas. I was told only yesterday by a thoroughly reliable source that an 11-pound parcel sent to Greece from Canada requires the payment of $3.10, but if it is sent from the United States the charge is only half that much, or $1.55. An air mail letter from Canada to Greece costs sixty cents; from the'United States it costs from twenty to thirty cents. We have all heard of the dire shortage of food in Greece, where the need is perhaps as great as or greater than in any other part of the world, and I believe that some steps might very well be taken to make it easier and cheaper for the sons of Greece in this country to send food to their starving relatives at home. If my information be correct, as I believe it is, I suggest that the department, which I have alw-ays found ready to act on what they believed to be reasonable suggestions, might look into this matter and see if it cannot be corrected.

I do not question the statement made by the hon. gentleman. The United States have direct lines ploughing the ocean between Greece and their seaports. We have not, so that we have to pay for the transit, which they do not have to do.

W'hat is the policy of the department with respect to the construction of new post offices? I gather that at the moment you are not doing much at it?

Supply-Post Office
No.
In the estimates before us I see nothing for capital expenditures. What is the pdlicy of the department with respect to the construction of new post offices?

The expenditure on buildings is, of course, made by the Department of Public Works. We requisition them and they build the post offices for us. We have established a rule, which is not inflexible, that we would construct post offices in towns having a net revenue of $10,000 or more; and as soon as we start building those we shall begin with the largest towns or cities and work down. That is our rule to-day, to build only where the net revenue is $10,000 or more.
I must answer the question asked by the hon. member for Rosedale in regard to the revenue of the philatelic service. For the year 1945 the number of orders received was 1,873, which brought a total of $142,740.
The Postmaster General says the Department of Public Works constructs the post offices. I presume they do so at the request or on the recommendation of the Post Office Department?
Yes.
Are you planning on building any post offices this fiscal year?

A few, in places where it is absolutely necessary. Those amounts will be provided in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Public Works.
I hope hon. members will understand that if they ask me questions in regard to post offices that are not very large I may not be able to answer them until I get the particulars from the officials of my department. I have in mind particularly post offices like the one mentioned by an hon. member from British Columbia. Every time a matter of this kind is brought to our attention we ask for a report from the superintendent of the district, and if the building is not what it should be we see that better service is given, especially where the postmaster has to furnish the premises.
Would the minister be prepared to say, perhaps at a later time, the amount of business done at Flin Flon, Manitoba?
Yes, I have that now. For the fiscal year 1944-45, which are the latest figures we have, the revenue was $32,667.

Then, under the policy of the department that town would be in line for
the construction of a post office, as soon as you commence construction on any scale?
Mr. BERTRAND (Laurier) [DOT] Yes. We have a list of those places, and I remember that Flin Flon is on the list.

The reason I ask is that for twenty years it was in the constituency I represented. They have made representations to me to see that their position is kept before the department.
