It is a city of ten thousand, doing a business of $30,000 a year, and the post office is still in very small, rented quarters. They tell me that place is in what the department calls a class A district. I presume they have districts classed as A, B, C and so on, and that class A means the class of towns which will be first to have buildings constructed when you decide to go ahead with them. Is that right?
That is correct.

During the war there have not been many extensions of rural routes. It seems to me the department should now consider extending rural routes into districts where they are badly needed. I hope the minister will give encouragement to the doing of this work.
How are revenue postmasters appointed? Are they appointed by the civil service commission? Is there any way of getting superannuation for postmasters who have given many years of service?

Revenue postmasters in offices making more than $3,000 in revenue are appointed by the civil service commission. Under that amount they are appointed upon recommendation. In every instance where there is a returned man we are giving preference to him, if he wants the job.
You are supposed to.
We always do.
I know cases where, not many years ago, that did not happen.
That was "not many years ago".

Has the department
considered any scheme for providing superannuation for the postmasters in smaller post offices?

This is a matter of policy which is being discussed to-day by the association of revenue postmasters. I do not know how it could be done. I understand that it would be difficult of accomplishment, but the question is being studied.
Supply-Post Office

It is only on rare occasions that I bring to the floor of the house problems concerning my constituency. During this question period, however, there are two or three matters I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General. The first of these is the need for additional letter carriers in the town of Pembroke. I am asking the Postmaster General to look into the situation there with a view to rectifying what I think is a grievance.
Then, has the minister up to this point given any consideration to taking care of people living on side-lines on which perhaps only two families live? I have always been confronted with the ruling that in order to have an extension there must be at least three families on three-quarters of a mile.

I said a few minutes ago that we were asking to have four families per mile, or one-quarter of a mile per family. Hon. members will realize that we cannot deliver rural mail in a place, for instance, where there might be only one family in three miles. That would cost too much. In such instances we ask the persons affected to come to a point near at hand where the rural mail passes, and to have their box at that point so that they can be served.
I shall look into the facts concerning Pembroke. The hon. member will understand that we give a letter-carrier service to towns with a revenue of $40,000 or more. If the hon. member wishes to set the facts out in a letter to me I shall be pleased to look into the matter.

In my constituency there are numerous cases of side-lines where perhaps only two families live, the nearest of which might be within half a mile of the comer. However it is a considerable hardship for those people to have to walk to that corner in all kinds of weather and to have to wait for the mailman. The mailman is not always on time.
Now that the war is over, I believe it would not be unreasonable to ask the Postmaster General to give relief in cases of that kind. I have numerous ceases which would fall into this class in my constituency. They have been getting their mail under these conditions through all these years, and their annoyance is growing all the time. The idea of having to walk half a mile through the snow or rain for their mail, when their neighbours have their mail delivered to their gates, does not appeal to them. After all, it is not so long ago that rural mail delivery was introduced, and I should think the time has come to 
extend the service. I suggest that this matter might be given most serious consideration so as to help these people who must endure considerable hardship in getting their mail.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question? I have been trying all night to do so, and I want to go home. Did I understand the minister to say that some small town in Manitoba is going to have a post office before Chilliwack gets one? Chilliwack has a revenue of $88,000, and it has the poorest service given in any post office on the North American continent. We have been endeavouring to get action from the minister's department for more than a year. I might add that the constituency is the best in Canada.
Despite our efforts to get action from the department, we have got absolutely nothing but a lot of very nice letters-which do not deliver the mail. The people have to stand in queues for three hours to get their mail in a post office bringing in a revenue of $88,000. We are told we cannot use the basement of the building because of something that happened many years ago in connection with the introduction of a stamp. And, by the way, I do not want a stamp, with the picture of a peach on it, or anything else. All I want is service for the post office. If the minister cannot answer to-night, I am not in a hurry. There is no hurry now to get the estimate through; we have been waiting all day. The minister knows all about the situation at Chilliwack.

This is a place which is on the list, and' which will be taken into serious consideration.
Mr. MaOlNNIS: Earlier in the evening when a question was asked about rural mail carriers I believe the minister answered that sometimes when tenders were called the lowest tender was less than the work could be done for. Under those circumstances, what is the policy of the department?

We know from experience that some tenderers are not going to make much money. But with the law as it is to-day, if the person who tenders is able and has the necessary apparatus, horses, automobiles or trucks to fulfil his contract, we have to give it to him. There is nothing in the law giving us discretion to eliminate the lowest tenderer.

But in a case where obviously the tenderer cannot fulfil the contract, and representations are made to the Post Office Department, how is the matter dealt with?

Supply-Post Office
We advertise for new contracts.

I should like to ask a question of the minister, and before doing so I want to tell him that I am not going to ask for anything on a stamp, not even the C.C.F. insignia. In reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Renfrew North, the minister said that a post office would require to have $40,000 a year revenue or more to warrant a mail-carrier service. In the important city of Swift Current in southwestern Saskatchewan the revenue is over $40,000 a year, and has been over that point for many years, and yet we have no mail-carrier service. It is not because we have not asked for it. A plebiscite was held in the town and the people asked for it. The Legion branch has asked for it in order that three or four men might be given work in performing a useful service for the city. Since we have a revenue of $40,000 and over, I should like to know what other reason there is for our not having this service.

When I said that we were giving carrier service to towns that had a revenue of $40,000 or more I did not mention that there are other conditions to be considered. A town must have at least
2,000	points of call because it takes that many to keep two or three letter carriers busy. I would not say that there should be a sidewalk for every foot over which a letter carrier would walk, but we do ask that the letter carrier be able to do his job without having to face possible illness owing to mud and water and so forth.

Mud does not bother us a great deal. In the last survey it was found there were 1,600 points of call on sidewalks, and there were also some other points of call on cinder walks. Those walks do not get very muddy. The 1,600 points of call would keep a couple of men busy.

Mail leaving the parliamentary post office does not reach Toronto until the second day after mailing. I do not see why there should be any delay because mail is sent through the parliamentary post office.

Could the minister break down this item and tell us how much he is going to pay to each company, and the rate that was paid during the last fiscal year?

In 1945-46 we paid the Canadian National $3,660,000, and
the Canadian Pacific, $4,037,000; we paid other lines $413,000, and there is another item of $2,396, making a total of $8,113,598.
Will the figure for this year be about the same?

Do you pay the same rate to the Canadian National as you pay to the Canadian Pacific?
Yes, exactly the same.

Item agreed to.
263. Air and land mail services, $18,571,767.
What is the basic rate per mile for air mail?
1-5 mills per pound mile.
What was the previous rate?

Forty-two
cents per mile and we changed the base completely to a pound-mile base.

I know of a firm which made application for an air route, but they were turned down, one reason being that they could not bid low enough to get an airmail contract. This particular concern points out that when the T.C.A. first started operations the rate was nearly four times what it is to-day and the present rate makes it difficult for small concerns to get going. Apparently the T.C.A. received -6 cents per mile throughout the first four years of its operations. At the present time companies other than the T.C.A. are receiving in the neighbourhood of [DOT]5 cents per mile. Is there any distinction in the rates in British Columbia and other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed that there is none whatever.

Will consideration be given - to increasing the rate in view of the fact that apparently it took a -5 rate for the T.C.A. to get going, whereas it is now -15, which makes it difficult for these small lines to get going?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As acting Postmaster General I shall be glad to bring the representations made by my hon. friend to the attention of my colleague and I am sure they will receive every possible consideration.

I have one question to ask and I do not know whether I should have asked it of the last Postmaster General or

Sup-ply-Post Office

the new one. Has consideration been given to providing an airmail service to Norway-House, Berens River, Grand Rapids and Warrens Landing during the winter time? It is essential that this service be provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are giving continuous and anxious and sustained consideration to the development of these routes.

I am told that on many occasions rural mail has been held up because it sometimes takes half an hour to open the mail bags because the locks will not open. At times they have to use a hammer and a few cuss words to get them open.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That may be the fault of the receiver as well as the dispatcher.
I wonder if the Postmaster General would check up on that and have the locks fixed.

I must tell the hon. gentleman that during the war we were unable to have bags made out of good cotton and we used almost anything we could find. There was a great increase in the mail during the war and we had difficulty in getting not only locks but everything that goes with the bags. The hon. gentleman will see that we are asking for quite a large amount of money this year to replace our stock of bags. I am not surprised that something might have happened because we had to take almost anything during the war.
I worked on one of these locks for half an hour, and at last had to use a hammer and then got the bag open.

In the railways and shipping committee when dealing with T.C.A. there was considerable questioning in connection with the rate which was paid by the post office to T.C.A. for air mail. T.C.A. seemed quite happy over the rate they are now getting, although it has been reduced from former years, because they are no longer under the thumb of the Post Office Department. as to the flights they must make. Is the Post Office Department equally satisfied with the rate which they pay to T.C.A.? I have not the figures, but I understand that that rate is considerably in excess of the rate paid in the United States for air mail. I notice in the estimates that the total amount for airmail service is greater than the amount for railway mail service, although the distances are extremely disproportionate.

We have only one route, and that is east-west or west-east. The post office wanted to help T.C.A.

establish itself when it was just starting up in Canada. Now it has passed that stage and we have made a contract on a pound-mile basis, which is the logical way of paying for air-mail service. We are paying a good price, one and a half mills per pound-mile, which is quite a lot. I must admit that it is more than is being paid for express and more than is paid for passengers. Passengers pay $6 for 200 pounds going 100 miles, which works out at about 3/10ths of a mill per pound-mile. We are paying for the air mail 1-5 mills per pound-mile. But that is on a decreasing scale. It comes down in four or five years at the end of the contract to -9 mills. We are reducing our airmail payment by about $50,000 a month.

For the last two years we spent $350,000 a year on mail bags, and this year the expenditure is $650,000. Would the minister give us some idea of the number of bags purchased and the reason for this large increase in expenditure?

During the war we could not manufacture or get any mail bags, and those conditions prevailed for five years, so that we did run short quite a bit. We have to replenish what we call our bank of bags. In Toronto alone during the Christmas season it takes 600,000 bags to handle the mail. Of course that is the largest post office we have in Canada.
They believe in Santa Claus in Toronto.

We have to replenish our bank and the bags are then distributed amongst the post offices throughout Canada. Last year we had to send out some of the mail in empty flour bags. During the Christmas season we shipped thirty-five carloads of mail from Toronto and, as I said, it took 600,000 bags just for that city. We have asked for tenders from the different cotton mills, and the only company which accepted a contract to furnish us with 10,000 yards of cotton per week was the Dominion Textile company. It will take at least six months before we have the number of bags we would have in ordinary times.
How many yards of cotton does it take for a bag? That would give us some idea of how much a bag costs.

The bags cost about $2. We buy the bag, the lock and everything, and we have the bags manufactured by two different companies, one in Montreal and one in Toronto.

Supply-Public Works

I am happy to be in agreement with the hon. member for Skeena for once when he brought up the subject of airmail service to the Queen Charlotte islands, which is relevant to conditions existing in my own riding. When I go to the Post Office Department I find a courteous minister and courteous assistants, but when you mention airmail service on some route where none is operating they look at you like a banker from whom you are trying to borrow money. I would point out to the minister that in providing an airmail service for these frontier points he is doing a great service for Canada, and I do not think we should penalize them to the extent we have in the past and expect them to put up with a lot of disabilities. Some help is needed from the dominion government. I should like the minister to give the assurance that negotiations are still proceeding with the Canadian Pacific and also with the charter lines that the hon. member for Skeena mentioned.
We are negotiating with these companies.

Will the minister explain this item? I ask for an explanation because the amount is so insignificant in view of the large number of employees in the Post Office Department. Would the minister also say whether the employees of the Post Office Department come under the Government Employees Compensation Act?
Yes, they do.

Chief architect's branch-
29\. Public buildings generally-repairs, alterations, fittings and improvements, $300,000.

I think this item includes the building which seemed to be going by so quickly and which I wanted to catch as it went by. Are there any anticipated changes or improvements in the near future under contemplation by the government with respect to the buildings here?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):

speechtext: No, not this item.

Where in these estimates is the item for post offices?
Mr. FOURNIER (Hull); They are pretty much all along. It is under "public buildings"; we have passed a good many of them as we went along this evening, and I was surprised that I did not get more requests, but really this year it has been the policy of the government not to put up new post offices. In certain instances we may acquire sites for future post offices, but it was represented to the Department of Public Works that the government wanted to keep all the materials we had for construction of housing, and we have taken a back seat this year and did not recommend any construction, so that the government's housing programme can be proceeded with. Next year we hope we shall have some new buildings. We know the state in which some of our buildings are right now; we know that new buildings are needed in many places. We admit that. But we thought the first priority should go to housing, particularly housing for veterans.
Is the minister saying that there is no provision in his estimates for the construction of new post offices in this fiscal year?

Well, I would not know exactly. I have in mind right now only one case where we may let the contract this year, and that would be at Sault Ste. Marie. We are acquiring the site now and preparing the plans and having specifications made, and that will not be only for a post office; it will be a general public building. I was out there myself to make a personal inquiry, and I find that a building is needed not only for postal services but for all the government services we have in the district. We are repairing a good many post offices this year, but I do not believe that any contract for new construction will be let during the fiscal year. As I have said, we shall acquire sites and prepare plans, but as to actual construction I do not suppose that before next spring we can get materials. I have in mind an instance where
Supply-Public Works

we gave out a contract, not for a building, but for a wharf, and we could not even get timber to proceed with that work at this time.

Before the last items of the minister's estimates are passed, will he give us a definite statement as to what post offices, if any, he contemplates building this year? He has said, practically none. What sites has he purchased, expecting to build immediately, and what post offices has he plans for constructing?

If my hon. friend will refer to pages 34 and following of the estimates he will see that, in Nova Scotia, we have at Halifax a postal station, North End, $25,000. and a Halifax office building, revote last year $50,000, total $100,000. All this work will not be done during the current year, and it is only a partial vote; it is not a complete vote for the whole building. In New Brunswick, there is Saint John, office building, revote of $50,000 from last year to this year; Saint John post office, alterations, and Sussex public building, $15,000 et cetera. As you go over the list you will find every item as to which expenses will be made this year, on pages 34 to 38 inclusive and part of page 3ft. Everything is there, and I cannot go farther than is mentioned on these pages in these items.

The hon. member has said that in some cases this is a revote of moneys appropriated last year. How are we to know whether this is just a figure in a book this year, or whether it is to be a post office?

It is all mentioned. As to going ahead, the session last year closed on December 16, if I recall well, and the votes which were passed at that time could not 'be expended on account of the late season. We now have the revote in these estimates; but part of that money may have been spent in preparing the plans and specifications.
Then the minister does expect to spend all the money for which he is now asking for these purposes in this fiscal year?

I cannot even go as far as that, because I cannot tell right now if, even with the projects we contemplate, we shall have the necessary materials to proceed. We may not expend all the money that is asked for in these items: it will depend on the supply of labour and materials.

Under item 234, public buildings, I want to ask the minister what he intends to do to improve these facilities in our

city.' If we take into consideration the revenue the department derives, something better might be expected. The various departments of government are scattered over a distance of seven or eight miles, and there seems to be no way of finding out how to get in touch with them by telephone. I have tried for many hours to locate particular offices for which I was looking. There should be a general public building. The need of such a provision in our city is urgent. The offices are old and dilapidated. Surely, with the revenues obtained by the post office we should have some new equipment, because business men are complaining that they cannot find offices which, like the income tax branch, are spread all over the city. Contrast this with any of the public utilities. The Bell Telephone, the gas company and all these other corporations provide fine offices for the convenience of the public. I can tell you, although the Minister of Veterans Affairs may smile, that it is not good enough. The business men of the country are kicking, and I should like to know if there is to be an improvement.

Item agreed to.
